children.title: On the magic of spoken language

blocks.text: The human beings are the only one that are given the power of spoken language. We are the only species who can articulate. This unique human ability is called by Mario Montessori: the magic of language. He asks the educators to think about it in this way. As educators we should bring the best of everything and not the worst, he says. Mario Montessori said that there is a modern tendency of asking for the minimum rather the maximum effort from the children, this implies that the human being is lazy, unintelligent and uninterested. When we look at the history, we as educators, should not be afraid of introducing more than just “a few” words to the children. If the school subjects would be offered as they should be than we would see what the human beings are capable of and in the children of how much work are these capable of.

We have to understand what we possess in our language, as it seems that at the moment we are seeking only for the basic language. The present attitude might seem that we reduce the language to a minimum, as we think that the words weight on the children. We don’t realize that we inherited the wealth of so many millions of souls who have lived before and left us a sort of magic.

The magic of words is brings us out of obscurity and solitude. Language is essential to become conscious, to socialize and to feel part of a group. The words/language gives us identity. Every word has the power to bring a picture in the mind of the person who understands. With a few words expressed by someone else you can be filled with emotion. You can feel the vibrations of another soul, even if you are far distant from the actual place that’s being recounted, you can see through the words what is happening and how is happening. That is magic.

We are becoming indifferent to the magic as we started to reduce the number of words used to a minimum, but each word is a living monument to some unknown person. He or she suffered or has been overtaken by joy that he / she created a sound
r series of sounds that were accepted by the others with gratitude and passed on
from generation to generation. When no words exist it is though as the human being is suffering. A human being can express with the help of the words its joy, rage, terror
r any other emotions.
The animals communicate between themselves but the difference is that the human beings do it with the help of the articulated language.

As long as the human beings had a soul/psyche but no language he might have felt imprisoned. We can’t go back to the early time of the species but there are situations when we can feel in a similar situation, for example while moving across the globe to a place where no one can speak our language or by thinking of a young child before being able to speak.

It takes tremendous effort to break the silence and release a sound that will be accepted by the community. From that moment the community takes that sound with enthusiasm and uses it to describe the same emotion/object.

When a human group takes a set of sounds, and associates it with a meaning, from that moment that set of sounds will passed over from generation to generation. Words can be forged and created in the heat of the emotion, meanwhile other words are created cold bloodedly. Science may require a new word, so we resort to Greek or Latin language which were almost extinct, but these languages live through the new words created from them. The very first words had been created as a result of the strong emotions that made the other people feel the same. There are other words which are imitative, imitating the sounds of nature – onomatopoeic. A group of people might have heard that sounds so they associated them with the object/being. (E.g. crack (sounds of something breaking) – to crack).

Every word is a vibration of a soul that it is passed onwards. Language is a series of monuments to people who are dead but whose gift will never die. This is how precious the words are. Words are monuments to the people who lived and forged them out
f the silence. We should be worthy of the precious gift that we were given, as words
are not pebbles but diamonds.

The hunger for words still exists between the ones that are still poor, there are still people who take words as gifts. They feel joy in receiving something they didn’t possess before, they seek for something they lack and want to know more. Words are appreciated by the ones that understand their value, for the others are just a burden. Sometimes in the process of education the educator will try to relive the students from this burden by making the things easier for the children. We should not reduce something as beautiful as the language to a burden.
The children are the ones who preserve the language and pass it on. Language evolves, new words come into existence and other words go into extension. Language is like a living organism.

children.title: On overview with the help of the AMI chart

blocks.text: This chart has been published in the AMI communications in n.2/1960

The first part numbered with 1 refers to the birth, the second part numbered with 2 refers the activities done by the child before reading. The ability of writing is in the centre (the doorway to reading) and the right part numbered with 4 refers to the activity of reading from the age of 7 to 8 – elementary child.
We can call the four parts of the chart as it follows:
Part 1: Birth and the first development of language
Part 2: Before the mastery of written language
Part 3: The doorway to reading
Part 4: Total reading
Part 1: Birth and the first development of language
The timeline for the spoken language

This chart as well as the four planes of development starts with the flame that represents the birth. It is graded for each month for the first two and half years of the child’s life. The first four months are considered the myelination, the period in which the nerve cells connect and start to function correctly (are being covered with a fat layer). At two months the child will turn at the sound of the voice, at four months he will look at the mouth that speaks and at six months he will start to repeat syllables again and again. The child is surrounded by sound in his environment, but what attracts him is the sound of the human voice. This is a sign of a sensitive period for language. Between six and ten months the child will continue with babbling. Around ten months the child will become aware that the sounds have meaning. By the time he is one year old, the child will say the first intentional word. At 15 months the child will start “baby talking” with a lot of vowel words and will try to imitate the words pronounced by the adult. At this age the child will understand the sense expressed in language. By the time of 18 months the child will start using names, he uses nouns.

Between 18 months to 21 months the child won’t use grammar but he will use words that might have multiple meanings. From 21 months the child will start using sentences. Before the age of 2 the child will start using adjectives, nouns, suffixes, prepositions, verbs and other parts of speech. Between the age of 2 and 2 and a half the child will express himself with a variety of phrases, sentences and even complex sentences. Around the age of 2 and a half the language will be complete. Enrichment, refinement and development will be still continue in the next years of life. The power
f understanding of a language by the child should never be underestimated.
Schematic diagram of the development of language
This chart symbolizes the development of the language from the early nebulae to the
rganized syntax that he/she will acquire. The nebulae stage is represented by the

cloud like forms that represent the potential of the child. In the first months of life the child sorts out the sounds that exist in his native language. At 6 months comes the first syllable and up to 8 months there is an unconscious attempt to form words (mechanical babbling). At 10 months the sounds have meanings, by the age of 1 year old comes the first intentional word. Around 14 months 2-syllable words with diffused meaning appear amidst vowels and interjections. At the age of 18 months everything has a name and between 18 months and 21 months there is a stage of babbling of sentences some with diffused meaning. At 21 months the nebulae come to an end. Between 21 months and 24 months there is an explosion of words and after the age of two the syntax is acquired and the speech has order and meaning. Don’t think about what causes the behaviour but think of where it is leading to - leading to development.
“In the universe exist two great categories of phenomena, the first called entropic have their origin or cause in the past and from the complicated, from the complex

proceed towards the simple, the uniform. An enormous class of different phenomena are phenomena which are driven by centre /original not back in past but in the future a centre of origin that reveals itself as the aim purpose or goad of the phenomenon. These phenomena are syntrophic phenomena. All phenomenon
typically are syntrophic phenomenon. In contrast the entropic phenomenon proceeds from what is simple, homogenous to the complex and differentiated.”
Luigi Fantappie

Children can’t get the language through the television before the age of two. There are three enemies for the children’s development: time (as we are always in a hurry), transport and television (screens).

We can help with the development of language with speaking in a clear way or with the help of rhythm and pitch. Also there is a musical aspect of the language, prosody, which has to do with the tone, intonation, rhythm and stress. The musical aspect of language is extremely important for the baby (E.g. the way adults speak to the children and the nursery rhymes).
Part 2: Before the written language (the years in the Children’s House)

We think about the period after the acquisition of spoken language and before the mastery of written language. It is a time of constructive perfectionment, refining and enrichment of language which will take place naturally. There are things that we can do to help the child enrich his vocabulary. For the Sensorial area in Children’s House we can give the proper language with the correct and complete terms (E.g. small and big, thin and thick, long and short, tall and short, colour names). The exactness of the meaning is offered with all these words, an important tool for the child to precisely describe the world that surrounds him/her.

In Children’s House there are many classified pictures that are going to become classified reading. One type has to do with the general environment and everyday life. (E.g. the rooms of the house, gardening tools, transportation etc.). Other type has to do with the scientific terms (E.g. botany). The classification of the pictures/cards it is very important. The fact that are classified means that there is always a meaning for context. These cards prepare the child for the written language in the future.

Stories, poems, nursery rhymes are all important for the development of the language and are always introduced by the adult. We should always think if the content is appropriate, if this content is based on reality or not. From Maria Montessori’s point of view we should not confuse the children with what’s true and untrue.
Building stories around a central theme i.e. the question game, as this helps with learning to building sentences in a logic way.

The environment should have a book corner as a way to acquire an attitude of love and respect for the books and reading. Practical help can include washing their hands, showing them how to handle the books, turn the pages and even how to fix them in case some become damaged. The book corner should be as comfortable as possible to feel as a real part of a home.

Self-confidence can be built by having a daily news time where the children can take turns and speak out in front of an audience. Respect and social grace can be taught also through these kind of activities from a very young age.
Preparation for the written language

Written language has two aspects: writing and reading. Certain preparation for writing is going to take place in Children’s house. There is indirect preparation of the hand for writing taking place in practical life area and in the sensorial area. The goal is to have the hand become obedient of the mind. In the practical life area we can mention the dressing frames, polishing, cleaning a table or even pouring. In the sensorial area the pincer grip is present in a variety of works like the cylinder blocks, the geometric cabinet and even while building the pink tower. Some sensorial materials have as a direct aim the preparation for writing, for example the metal insets (preparation of the hands), the sandpaper letters (preparation of the hand and mind) and the movable alphabet (from words to symbols).
Part 3: The doorway to reading

The doorway to reading is also the doorway to culture and understanding. Our society places a great emphasis on literacy as well as the Montessori education. The written language is the key to culture as this is how knowledge is preserved. Written language it is considered to be essential to all our members of the society including the children. It is not enough to have the spoken language, two languages are required: the spoken language and the written.
Archaeologists look at objects from the prehistoric time as a way to construct the human story because humanity doesn’t have any written evidences of the events that might have passed in those times.
Part 4: Total reading (the children in Elementary)

Complete mastery of the mechanical process. At the beginning of the evolution of the written language we had “picture writing” – pictograms and with the time we evolved to have signs for sounds – phonograms. Some are diagraphs phonograms with double letters (E.g. “sh”, “ch”, “th”). In this part of the language training for English there is also a “puzzle words” activity which doesn’t exist for other language like Italian for example. Also we have reading activities that help the children to enrich their vocabulary and understand the meaning of words.

For reading, to become total reading it is not enough to have only the mechanical process and the rich vocabulary but we also have to understand the function of the words. To appreciate the function of words there are activities that help the children to understand the function and the importance of the position of the words. The importance of the work is to make the children aware/conscious of the language that they speak. The ability to interpret the thoughts and feelings of the author. To help with this task in the elementary environment we have activities for the reading analysis and the interpretive reading slips. For the general word consciousness there is the word study (suffixes, prefixes, compound words and the word families). The children learn to use the library and how to use a dictionary or an encyclopaedia. For the written expression there is the creative writing and the written question game.
In the environment there should be available for the children literature of good quality that will ensure that a rich vocabulary is used with a correct punctuation.
“Total reading means that the child should grasp the completeness of what is written, not only in term of understanding but also for style and sentiment of what he
reads. In order that he can make harmonious sense out of an attractive forest of thoughts we most give him the possibility of total reading. Few are total readers as
the mind is not trained for it. You have to guide the mind step to take from the reading the totality of what’s expressed. “
Mario Montessori
Elementary language study
Word studies: prefixes, suffixes, compound words, word families
Grammar boxes (reading boxes)
Sentence analysis
Story of the spoken language
Story of the written language: The ox and the house
Classification of the parts of speech
Clause analysis (Sentence analysis)
Study of style (the different genres of literature and the child’s own style)

children.title: Sandpaper letters
Vowels and consonants

blocks.text: Each letter represents a sound of our language so we can think of them as a phonogram. The alphabet represents a great human achievement that simplifies the human language. Letters make written language easy, so easy, and so simple that written language becomes accessible to everyone, not just a few scribes. The written language began with the pictograms which were much complicated than the letters of the alphabet. For the sand paper letters, each letter is separated, each is cut in sandpaper and the work is designed especially for the sensitivity of the young children that love to touch and trace. The cursive letters should be in the style of cursive for the country where the school is. Cursive comes more naturally to the hand and the letters are easier to distinct.
The word vowel comes from the Latin word for voice. The word consonant comes from “sounding with” in Latin.
Because the sandpaper letters are going to be presented with the sound of the letter, the fact that the English is not phonetic language – emerges very fast.
There are also wall charts available so the children can see the correct placement
f the letters with the letters made of sandpaper.

The 26 letters of the alphabet, each of them on a smooth board with the letter made out of sandpaper. The consonants have a blue background and the vowels have a red background. The letters are in cursive.
The guide will ask the child to sensitize its fingers (by washing with warm water
r rubbing together).
The guide chooses one sandpaper letter, places it on the table and holds it with the left hand if the he is right handed.
First period:
The guide traces the letter with two fingers and says the sound of the letter, twice.
Now he invites the child to trace and say the sound.
Second period:
The guide will ask the child to trace a letter by saying the sound of the letter.
Third period:
The guide will ask the child to trace and say the sound of the letter.
At first the guide will introduce 3 contrasting letters (E.g. a, t, v).
The first step is to introduce the phonetic sounds to the child. Each letter will be associated only with one sound.
The 26 letters have 23 sounds as some sounds repeat (c-k, q – mute, x – cs)
Sound games should come before the sandpaper letters.
Always encourage the child to trace during the three periods. The tracing helps the child to develop a muscular memory.
With all the work with the sandpaper letters and the metal insets is properly completed we will have the chance to see a beautiful handwriting.

children.title: Movable alphabet

blocks.text: There are two schools of thought about when to start with the movable alphabet: after introducing all the sandpaper letters or before the children know all the sandpaper letters and diagraphs. Maria Montessori thought the movable alphabet can be introduced while still working with the sandpaper letters.

The child is ready to start working with the movable alphabet when he is interested to put sounds together. The beauty of this material is that children can take words that they know and form them using the letters. It is a way for the child to refine his spoken language. The child is free to form all the words he wishes. If the child asks for a word from the adult, the adult should offer a phonetic word.
A box with the cut out letters of the alphabet with many copies of the same letter. Some boxes come also with punctuation marks.
Mat with lines for writing
Presentation for the special 6 years old

Conclusion for writing in Children’s House/Special 6 years old
The children in Children’s house are expected to move spontaneously from the sandpaper letters, movable alphabet and metal insets to writing with a pencil.
There are signs when the children are ready to move on, to writing with a pencil:
They can easily make parallel strokes
They can trace easily the sandpaper letters
They have a certainty and readiness with working with the movable alphabet

The adult should wait at least a week before the child is ready to start writing spontaneously. The adult can use blackboards with lines for writing. If the child hesitates to write a specific letter, the adult should encourage the child to go back to the sandpaper letters. The child prepares himself for writing without writing, it is not taught to write by writing. With the special 6 years olds we should use the same approach and if they are not very interested, additional activities may be used like coloring, sewing to improve the motor skills.

In the “Formation of man” Maria Montessori writes that written language can be acquired much more easily by children who are 4 years old that 6 years olds. When and how the things are offered truly maters. It has to be kept in mind that spoken and written language form a unit together.

Active writing is a complex ability, be it in Children’s house or Elementary, so it has to be broken in simpler activities. For an elementary child the guide needs to think what kind of interesting activities we can offer. The hand has to be able to do precise, minute drawings, to be light, to do flowing movements. We can call this in general: manual dexterity.
In the book Formation of man, Maria Montessori it is interested how this same materials can be used to train even adults to learn to write.

For the special 6 year olds, there is a special story called “The Ox and the house”. The letters have a story and that makes it interesting for the older child, for this purpose the first work to use is the movable alphabet. After some interest has been created the sandpaper letters can be introduced and later the metal insets.

Creating interest always helps to overcome the obstacles. Maria Montessori had a chart on the wall with all the vowels marked in red so the children could feel encouraged as it is very probable that they might know many.

We can use three letters from the movable alphabet (2 consonants, 1 vowel) and try to make some words that the child can read. We try to encourage the child that even with such a few letters he already knows a lot.
Short introduction of the language history
The written language begins with picture writing, pictograms. In Africa it was used as a form of communication and it still used today in different ways: signs and emoji all
ver the world.

As the written language developed it started to depend on the spoken language, and with this the evolution of signs started to be associated with the sounds (phonograms). In the early stage phonograms were used to represent syllables then when the signs started to represent a specific sound we got the alphabet.

The alphabet is a limited number of signs that combined can express an unlimited number of ideas. Maria Montessori had a clear phonic approach at the beginning, going from sounds to letters, it means the focus is on the sounds not on the words. The alphabet is the key to the written language to become accessible, therefore the first approach is phonic.
A phrase is an incomplete thought (E.g. long rod, blue tree, great mountain). As soon as the child starts to write phrases, the words have to have spaces between them.

When the children move on to sentences we need to introduce the punctuation. When we have a complete thought, we have to make it clear that it is a complete thought. We can “decorate” the complete thought with a punctuation mark.
For the older children words are not so interesting they would like to write phrases or sentences.
While forming words with the movable alphabet it is very easy to rearrange the letters and correct mistakes, as opposed to correcting written mistakes on paper.

children.title: Word reading

blocks.text: For the special 6 years olds any activity offered for writing also brings a connection to reading. For a Children’s House child writing comes before reading. Maria Montessori used the word “explosion” for these acknowledgements for the child as it shows the energy that involves when this moment comes into the life of the young child. For the
lder six year olds there aren’t going to be any explosions and the passage from
writing into reading is slow and laborious. For the older children writing and reading comes all together.

The writing and reading processes are concerned with the correlation of the mind and the hand. First the mind breaks the word into sounds and finds the corresponding letters for those sounds. For reading the opposite happens and the mind will look for the sounds corresponding to the letters. For the process of writing there is no urgency meanwhile for reading there is an urgency required in sounding out the letters to make any sense for us. Reading is a process of synthesis (putting the sounds together).
Having in mind the difficulties for reading as opposed to the ones of writing we can understand why a young child will start writing before reading meanwhile for a child
ver 6 years old these processes may take time.
There are two levels for reading: reading of words and reading of sentences.

children.title: Functions of words

blocks.text: With the functions of words (parts of speech) we can explore the grammatical element of the language, this being part of the Montessori approach to reading. We can use grammar to help reading become total reading, a quality reading focused
n the complete understanding of the text being read. If the children can speak their

mother tongue, they already know the structure of the language (the grammar of the language), our work is to make the children aware of the things they already know. Any help that is given to reading is indirectly a help to writing, the more a child reads the better he will write. As opposite of the idea that grammar is analysing and dismembering the language, the grammar study in the Montessori environment is a work of construction. The activities should be interesting for the children and offer a broader perspective of the language they speak. It is a work to help the children understand the value and importance of each word, a work of slow and reflective reading. The construction should come before analysis and we can think of an analogy, a person who builds a house understands it better than someone who takes it apart. What does “function of words” means? It is the task carried out, the role played by each kind of word in speech. We can classify the words according to the functions that the words have.

“The study of the functions of words, is a way of penetrating the language that already exists in the child. It is a means of perfecting and fixing the shape of its language, therefore this study of the language is very useful to the child who is in the
process of organizing the language of himself” Maria Montessori

The parts of speech in English are: noun, article, adjective, conjunction, preposition, verb, adverb, pronoun and interjection. The definite article is “the” and the indefinite articles are “a” and “an”. The noun, article and the adjective can be considered a family (“noun family”) as the article and adjective are always accompanied by a noun. Another family that we can think of it is the family made by the verb, the adverb and the pronoun (“verb family”).

children.title: Function of the noun

blocks.text: For the function of the noun we have a story called “The story of the multitude”. As we are having a story for the presentation, we can call it a psychological

children.title: Presentation

blocks.text: “Names are something full of life and secrets, they have something that enflames our curiosity. One must know them to love them and love them to
acquire an even more exact knowledge of them.” Maria Montessori

children.title: The story of the multitude

blocks.text: The multitude that we are thinking of is the multitude of names, it is the multitude
f ideas which the human mind has been able to perceive. All things have a
name, people, countries, the things that are made and all the things in nature, plants, stones and the animals known by humans, all have a name.

When the humans learned to navigate every type of vessel and each part of the boat had a name. And when the stormy seas opposed them, the obstacles and dangers, each one of these had a name. And when lightning, wind and thunder frightened them, the lightening, thunder and wind each had a name.
When the wild animals approached them and sometimes feeling afraid or hungry attacked them, all these animals, their movements, cries and howls had a name.

When the people thought about the ones that they are missing, when they loved, when they felt themselves consoled, each movement of the soul had a name. And when with the lens they began to see very tiny things invisible to the naked eye, the lens had a name and so had the instruments used for
bserving and so did the new tiny things they had seen with their instruments.

Each newly perfected thing that came into being had a name. If the human felt himself to be stronger, more intelligent, the increased strength and intelligence had a name. And if people making their life more complex, they experienced new feelings, these too had a name.
And from generation to generation the humans died, well, the names remained and accumulated.
And so it is, that if out of the immensity of the existing things some don’t receive a name, these things don’t exist for humans as they didn’t enter their consciousness.

children.title: After the story
Understanding of the story

blocks.text: The guide asks the children what they understood from the story - everything has a name.

children.title: Names in the environment

blocks.text: The guide will ask the name of different things until the child doesn’t know a name
The guide will say to the child that he will let the child know the name of that object without saying it – he writes it on a slip of paper and gives it to the child to read it

children.title: Handwritten slips with concrete and abstract nouns

blocks.text: The guide says that he will let the children find a names without saying them. The guide writes names on the slips of paper and ask the children to match them. (E.g. plant, class, table, thought). The guide talks about the fact that the noun “thought” cannot be matched with nothing physical.
Words that are used for naming, are called nouns. Noun comes from the Latin “nomen” = name. When the people say noun, they say names.
“The name or the noun is the spiritual substance or the essence of the things. Its substance becomes spirit. “Maria Montessori

children.title: Follow-up activities
Labels for the “Little environment”

blocks.text: The guide invites the child to work with the little environment and the labels
The guide reads the name on the label and says to the child that if the object could’ve heard it, he would’ve come – but as it can’t come the guide will go and take it.
The guide will invite the child to read the next labels and find the objects that correspond to that names

children.title: Read and write poems

children.title: Names of the children (proper nouns) and their particularities

blocks.text: The guide can read the names of the children and talk about the names and their particularities
This story was published in the Italian psychogrammar.
“Fairy tales” – by J.C. Cooper

In the book, J.C. Cooper says that in ancient times knowing the name of someone or something meant to have power over that person/thing. Those early societies were very conscious of the power of the names. Knowing the true name was thought that gave power over the soul. We can find examples in religion, myth, ritual, legends and fairy tales. (In the Christian religion it is restricted the use of the name of God – e.g. ten commandments). In the Roman times a man would receive his name when he became a man, a woman when she got married.
The names have power as the names represent cultures, identities and even personal characteristics.
To help the children to become aware of the naming of the words, to appreciate the value and importance of that words.
To help the child become aware that everything has a name
To help the child understand that a word used for naming is a noun
6-9 years old

bjects.

ther

bject

ut of several

“When we say he is “the teacher”, we mean that is personally him. If we say he is “a teacher”, we mean someone who has the profession of a teacher. One out of

many. This little word “a” is also an article but it is not used to determine or define but used to enumerate. A is anyone, one out of many, one of the immense multitude. The indefinite article is always single, the unit being the singular. “Maria Montessori

children.title: Adjective

blocks.text: The function of the adjective is to describe a noun, to distinguish or differentiate things that are similar, for the same thing at different times or for the pure pleasure of depiction to evoke a picture in someone’s mind. Mario Montessori talks about the work of the function of the adjective as a game, as the children already know the adjective.
Three real flowers, each of a different colour
Slips of paper
Black and red pencils
Solid symbols: three pyramids (black, dark blue, clear blue)
Flat symbols: three triangles (black, dark blue, clear blue)
Scissors

children.title: Presentation of the function
Handwritten slips with the adjective in red and three flowers

blocks.text: The guide places the three flowers
The guide writes on a slip with a gap “the flower” and asks the child to
bring it
When the child brings the red flower but the guide says it’s not what he wants
and writes on the slip of paper “the white flower” and gives it to the child to
bring it
The guide writes labels for the other two flowers: “the red flower”, “the yellow
flower”
The function of the word in red is to identify a particular flower.
The guide says to the child that “These special words in red describe the flower,
a word like that is called an adjective. Adjective comes from Latin which
means to add”

children.title: Presentation of the symbol
Introduction of the solid symbols for the noun family

blocks.text: The guide says to the child that to symbolize the adjectives we are going to use the pyramids

The guide explains to the child that we use the pyramid, as known from the small geometric solids. The guide continues that pyramids are stable, when made from stone the Egyptians wanted them to last forever. The names are like the pyramids, they last and last, they are lasting pyramids. The biggest one is large and black as coal (which is also very old) and it represents the nouns (names).

The guide analyzes the pyramids with the child: the colour and the size. There is one for each part of the speech that they have: the biggest for the noun, the middle one for the adjective and the smallest one is the article. They are a family, which is called as the biggest in the family – the noun family.
The guide shows to the child an image with the pyramids from the smallest to the biggest – left to right.

children.title: Introduction of the flat symbols for the noun family

blocks.text: The guide makes the trick and shows to the child the plain figures: the three triangles hidden on one side of the solid pyramids.
The guide invites the child to mark with the triangles the parts of speech of the slips of the flowers from the table.

children.title: Presentation of the transposition

blocks.text: The guide cuts the flower label and mixes the parts of speech to emphasize the importance of the order “the flower white”, “white the flower”, etc.
The guide returns to the original order and checks with the children the order
f the parts of speech on the other labels
The guide shows to the child an image with the family of the noun

A basket with labels with article, adjectives and nouns on each

children.title: The detective adjective game

blocks.text: Additional material required

A box with 54 triangles: 3 colours (red, yellow, blue), 3 sizes (large, medium, small), 3 different qualities of angle (right angled, obtuse angled, acute angled), 2 qualities of sides (isosceles, scalene).
Strips of paper for checking the sizes
Slips of paper for writing
Black pencil
A box with labels with all the adjectives written in black

children.title: Presentation with the handwritten slips

blocks.text: The guide invites the child to spread on mats all the 54 triangles
The guide talks with the child about the role of a detective
The guide says that he will give the child clues and writes on a piece of paper “the triangle”
The child brings a triangle
The guide gives another clue to the child “red”
The guide invites the child to sort the triangles according to the clue received. The child removes the triangles that don’t match the clue.
The child brings a red triangle but now the guide says that he has a new clue and write on a slip of paper “large”
The child has to sort the triangles according to the new clue, remove the
nes that don’t match the clue and when is done bring to the guide a
large red triangle.
The guide gives another clue to the child “scalene”
The child has to sort the triangles according to the new clue, remove the
nes that don’t match with the clue and when is done bring to the guide
a large red scalene triangle.
The guide gives another clue to the child “right-angled”
The child brings the red large scalene right-angled triangle.
The guide invites now the child to write “a report”, they take all the clues and put them in the correct order: “the large red right-angled scalene triangle”.
The guide invites the child to place the correct symbols.
The guide invites the child to work with the special labels already prepared.

children.title: Working with the prepared labels

ne by one and place them in the correct column.

blocks.text: The guide invites the children to glue down symbols for their poem.
It’s up to the guide’s choice to give to the children the name “adjective”
For the introduction of the symbol is important to wait until reaching the adjective in order to create more impact
In the past the adjective was called “addnoun”
The little environment should not be present at all the times in the classroom, rather can be unpacked when necessary
If we want to bring out the function there are different ways:
From absence to presence
By changing
From the presence to absence
To help the child become aware of the normal word order
To help the child become aware of the function of the adjective
To help the child make a deeper study:
With only adjective it is possible to distinguish one object out of several but more adjectives are required in order to distinguish one object out
f the large quantity of similar objects.
Adjectives cannot be placed at random with any noun.
To help the child become aware that the adjective, preposition and noun are part of a family – constitute a grammatical unity.

children.title: Conjunction

blocks.text: So far we have been working with a family of words, the noun family. Now there are going to take two further exploration: how things can be joined and how things relate one to another spatially, in terms of position.
2 flowers
Red ribbon
Slips of paper
Red and black pencils
The symbols for noun, article, adjective and conjunction

Handwritten slips with the conjunction in red and two flowers

blocks.text: The guide writes in black on slip of paper “the yellow flower” and on another “the white flower”
The guide asks the child to bring the object mentioned on the slip of paper
The guide writes on a piece of paper “and” in red
The guide puts the slips together so the child can read “the yellow flower and the white flower” and invites the child to tie the flowers with the red ribbon
The guide asks the children what word told them to put the flowers together
The child answers “and”
The guide says that this kind of word is called conjunction.

blocks.text: The guide invites the children to place the symbols that they already know
The guide introduces the new symbol for the conjunction.

blocks.text: The guide shows to the children different variations “and the yellow flower the white flower”, “and the white flower the yellow flower”, “the white flower and the yellow flower” and discuss together the possible variations and the correct place for the conjunction. In the case of the conjunction there are two correct versions.

blocks.text: Slips of paper

Black and red pencils

children.title: 1st Presentation of the verb (“The difference between energy and matter”)
Handwritten slips with nouns and verbs

blocks.text: The guide invites the children to take some large objects from the little environment and display them
The guide is writing on slips of paper nouns “doll”, “table”, “chair”
The children read the slips and place them correspondingly
The guide is writing on slips of paper different actions “sing”, “run”, “skip”

The guide says that these kind of words are called “verbs” – it comes from Latin word “verbum” for “the word” – it can symbolize that it is the most important word.

children.title: Introduction of the solid symbol

blocks.text: The guide brings the pyramid for the noun – and talks about the fact that a pyramid is stable, old, big, etc.

children.title: Introduction of the flat symbol

blocks.text: The next day the guide asks the children is they remember what it was written
n the slips of paper

bject is transitive while an action verb with no direct object is

The legend of “The flying Dutchman”: “She was an Amsterdam vessel and sailed from port seventy years ago. Her master's name was Van der Decken. He was a staunch seaman, and would have his own way in spite of the devil. For all that, never a sailor under him had reason to complain; though how it is on board with them nobody knows. The story is this: that in doubling the Cape they were a long day trying to weather the Table Bay. However, the wind headed them, and went against them more and more, and Van der Decken walked the deck, swearing at the wind. Just after sunset a vessel spoke him, asking him if he did not mean to go into the bay that night. Van der Decken replied: "May I be eternally damned if I do, though I should beat about here till the Day of Judgment." And to be sure, he never did go into that bay, for it is believed that he continues to beat about in these seas still, and will do so long enough. This vessel is never seen but with foul weather along with her. “
Verbs such as to run, to walk, to dance all of them describe ways of going, but the fundamental most natural way is to walk

Conclusion (“Theoretical considerations on activity”)

During Montessori’s life in the traditional school the children had only to sit, quietly and listen. In the modern education nowadays, there is a lot of movement but just for the sake of movement – without a purpose.

When it comes to a Montessori school there is a lot of movement, but the movement has purpose as it used in the educational process (purposeful movement) – activity as means of development. It is important to have an aim for the movement so often can have a point of consciousness.

In a Montessori classroom, movement is a help for the children’s physical development, but more importantly it has to be a help for the psychic life. If the activity provided are not in accordance with the development needs of that age, all this movement can be interpreted just as rest or amusement.

What distinguishes the Montessori schools from other modern schools is that it provides psychic activity with movement but as well without a lot of movement. The Montessori classroom should be an environment in which the children’s potentiality can develop.

The absence of movability as in the “Silent game” can be interpreted as a supreme state – superior to the normal state of things. The silence can also be interpreted as an opportunity for concentration.

children.title: Story of the written language

blocks.text: The piece of paper that sees and speaks

children.title: Presentation of the story (The piece of paper that sees and speaks)

blocks.text: The story is used to illustrate the power and magic of written language
The guide talks with the children about the fact that people move from a part
f the world to another. And when the people moved a long time ago they
would take seeds or animals with them. This story takes us in time to a faraway place.

Story: Once upon a time in a country far away, there was a gardener who succeeded in growing a pear tree after much effort. It was a type of pear tree that he had brought with him from the country where he was born. Naturally the tree had a hard time growing where it was hot all year long. Finally the tree bore fruit and the fruit ripened. So the gardener picked a bushel of pears for his friend. He called a messenger and asked him to take the basket together with a letter to the man’s friend, Rajesh. The messenger boy set off on his journey, but fearing he’d lose the letter, he put it under his hat. He had to walk a long way carrying this basket and the sun was very hot. The boy became thirsty and said to himself, “No one will notice if one pear is missing from this basket.” And he decided to eat one. When he reached his destination he gave the basket with fruit and the letter to Rajesh. The man took the letter, read it and asked the messenger why a pear is missing. The boy first denied the existence of the fruit but after a while he decided to be honest and asked the man how he knew about the missing fruit. The man replied that the little paper he brought, told him. The messenger completely amazed took a short look at the magical paper that could see without eyes and talk without mouth. The next week the boy was sent again with the same errand. Feeling thirsty again he now thought about eating one fruit, but this time he took a lot of caution, covered the paper with a big stone in a faraway bush, so that it cannot see or hear what he was doing. “Now, no one will know” - he thought. Once again at the destination the man asked the messenger for the missing fruit. He could not believe his ears – the little paper knew the truth. Frightened, the boy asked for forgiveness and implored the man to allow him to see it again. What great magic is this, the paper even when buried under a stone in a far far away bush it could see and say the hidden truth, this paper could talk without anyone hearing it. Ashamed he begged the man for forgiveness and went to tell to his friends about the magic that he just witnessed. The humble messenger saw the magic of the written language that many fail to see, and the next week he and all his friends came to the door of Rajesh and they said, “You have a magic gift, you can hear the piece of paper speak. Can we somehow pay you to teach us the magic of this wonderful gift?” As they are all standing in the front of the man’s door, he smiled at them and said: “This gift is beyond any price that I could name. This is a gift that I shall not sell, but I shall give for free. Because all people should have this gift, for it allows you to make papers around the world speak to you. This is the gift called reading. And this gift I shall give to you, your village, and your people without charge, fully from my heart, for it's something that all of us should have and will give us all great pleasure. It will give you pleasure just as it has gave me.”
To help the child understand the magic of the written language
6-9 years old

blocks.text: 6 series of books:
Series 6: Books with sentences and pictures (one of each per page). The content on each page not related with the one on the next page.
Series 7: Books with sentences and pictures (one of each per page). The content on each page not related with the one on the next page. Have a theme but no title.
Series 8: Books with sentences and pictures (one of each per page). The content on each page is related with the one on the next page. Have a specialized theme but no title.
Series 9: Books with one or two pages of direct speech in black and red, with the correct punctuation, except the punctuation for direct speech. No title.
Series 10: Books with one or two pages of direct speech all in black, with the correct punctuation, including the punctuation for direct speech. No title.
Series 11: Books with one or two pages of direct speech all in black with a narrator. No title.
Series 12: Printed books with a title (may include pictures)

children.title: Question games and Reading analysis
Introduction

blocks.text: Sentence analysis it is called logical analysis in Italian language, this is why Maria Montessori referred to it as logical analysis. There are two branches in the English language: Grammatical analysis (words) and sentence analysis. The aim is to help the children become conscious, appreciate and perfect their own language.

In the English language a sentence can be analyzed first to find the subject and the predicate. The verb is the most important part of the predicate. After identifying the subject and the predicate, we can look for the direct object or indirect object, adverbials, attributives, complements and appositives.

children.title: Parts of sentence in English language
Subject
Responds to the question:  “Who/What is it that…?”

blocks.text: The subject is the person or thing about which something is being stated.

children.title: Predicate
Responds to the question: “What’s the action?”

blocks.text: The predicate is the part of a sentence that tells something about the subject.

children.title: Direct Object
Responds to the questions: “What?” /”What?”

blocks.text: A direct object is a person or thing that is affected by the action of the verb. You could say that the direct object "receives the action of the verb." (E.g. “He broke the window.”)

children.title: Indirect Object
Responds to the questions: “To whom?” / “To what?” / “For whom?” / ”For what?”

blocks.text: An indirect object is a person or thing that the action is done to or for. The indirect
bject usually comes just before the direct object. You could also say that the indirect
bject is the receiver of the direct object. (E.g. “He gave his mother flowers”)

children.title: Adverbial

blocks.text: Responds to the questions: “How?” / “When?” / “Where?” / “Why?” / “What for?” /

children.title: Responds to the questions:  “How?” / “When?” / “Where?” / “Why?” / “What for?” / “With whom?”/ etc.

blocks.text: A word or phrase functioning as a major clause constituent and typically expressing place (in the garden), time (in May), or manner (in a strange way).

children.title: Attributive
Responds to the question:  “Which?” / “What kind of?”

blocks.text: Attributive is an adjective or adjectival phrase that modifies a noun and constitutes part of the same noun phrase, in English normally preceding the noun, as black in “Fido is a black dog” (as opposed to Fido is black).

children.title: Complements
Used with linking verbs

blocks.text: A complement is a word or a group of words (usually an adjective or a noun), that is used after linking verbs (such as be and become). The complement identifies or describes the subject of the verb. (E.g. “She seems very satisfied”)

children.title: Appositive/Apposition
Stays next to another noun in the subject (E.g. My teacher, Baiba Krumins, [...])

blocks.text: A relationship between two or more words or phrases in which the two units are grammatically parallel and have the same referent (e.g. my friend Sue; the first US president, George Washington). Stays next to another noun which is part of the subject.

No collective task could be completed without language that leads to understanding. These few sounds brought material and spiritual organization so that the best and worst in the human beings was reached. A breath somewhat longer than usual and there it came language. Do not destroy this
magic when you introduce language to children.

Reading and writing made the human being who was already magic into a God. I can make myself heard from one hill to another if my voice is loud enough, but through writing, I can make myself heard for thousand of years.”

[…] The phenicians, getting the idea from Egyptians, made these little despicle signs, they had these 22 myascrolls. Like nothing apparently, yet they kept alive whatever was noble in the mind of mind, whatever was considered great, worth keeping and transmiting. Only the worthy things were kept, those things that made an impression
n humanity. The spiritual capital of mankind was made from these 22 little
“misserable” signs, despicable signs as the Egyptians called them. The egyptian

priests have understood the miracle of writing and they resented its vulgarazation(make them available to everyone. We who are so accostumed to reading and writing, pay no attention to it. We do not realize the mirracle of written
language.

[…] Do not destroy the magic of the alphabet, the miracle of reading. Give the children the mirracle in all its force, let them absorb this whisper of one mind to another, the silent communion between people who are far away or from the ones
that are not with us today.
[…]I feel that we the teachers who have to transmit this gift, we have to realise its value, the great power the human beings gained. We must not treat the alphabet
as something despicable, as a collection of signs that you have to teach to the children. See how laborious were the steps that yeld to them. Let’s suppose
someone wants to give a message who is absent and he realizes that the wealfare

f all of his group, depens on that message. After following the movements of the enemy, how carrefully he will leave an arrow, a group of pebbles or hairs to be placed if the enemy came on horses. It is true that this one of way of
communicating, it is true that the silence can be broken in this way or the objects can be there days later but if you have to write Shakespeare in this language how
hard would it be. The human beings understood the necesity of using signs instead
f objects.
[…] The fascination of transmitting and fixing one’s ideas seems to be a need of the human soul. It is a need for the secret communication, the silent speech between

people. Children also often try to create secret languages which only they can understand. Adult, too, feel this need – they want to fix something worthwile. It should give the impression that, as when it is given the possiblity of hearing with the

children.title: Presentations of the “Story of the Ox and the House”
Tell the Cosmic fable

blocks.text: We are telling this new story today, the story it is called the Story of the Ox and the House. I’m not going to tell you why, because you are going to discover that by yourself. Meanwhile let’s have a look at this. [Show the movable alphabet] It is the movable alphabet, do you know how many letters are here? 26 (counts and says). We should say only 26, because 26 are not so many, because with that with these signs we can make all the words of our language. Can you imagine how many words are in the encyclopedia which is made up of so many volumes – hundreds of thousands. We can make every one of them with these 26 signs (letters) – from the shortest word, maybe just a letter, to the longest word of over 20 letters. No matter how long or short a word is, it is made with these 26 signs. Where did these letters come from? Did your parents invent them? Did the people of this country invented them? Maybe the Romans or the Greeks? If it wasn’t your parents, the English people, the Romans or the Greeks, then we have to go back even longer ago to understand how we got these letters. For this purpose I have to tell you a story:
The story of the ox and the house
[Put the movable alphabet away]

Let’s start by thinking of a time long long ago, let’s even start before the actual start of our story? Do you recall how the earth came to be and how humans finally came? And when the human beings came they were very poor, physically speaking. They had no sharp teeth, no claws to defend themselves, no fur coats for the cold, but they did come with some very special gifts. They came with some special gifts: a special mind for thinking, a special love and the third gift – the gift of hands? There is something else which is very special about the human beings, we can talk – I am talking right now. I can use my tongue to speak, I can tell you how I feel and right now I’m telling you a story. You can do the same, speak and tell me how you feel, if you like the story or not – we can communicate. We use spoken language. Long, long before anything was written down, people spoke. People spoke for a very long time before they could write anything down. Do you remember the timeline of the hand? Generations and generations of human beings were speaking without ever putting their thoughts down in writing. Just being able to speak to one another was absolutely wonderful. But think, there must have been situations when someone had to go away, and desperately needed to speak to someone who wasn’t there. In other words, someone was desperate to communicate and they can’t do it by speaking. Could they telephone? No, we are talking about a very long time ago, they didn’t even have paper and pencils, nothing that we use know. So how could they leave a message? Something they thought was really important they needed to communicate. What could they do? [Present chart 1 – Azilian pebbles]

Perhaps at first, they used objects for leaving messages. They could use stones, pebbles, feathers, perhaps a certain number of stones and pebbles could be left to say how many of the enemy were around. We have actually found painted pebbles. We don’t know what they mean, these pebbles date back to a long time ago, right back to the Old Stone Age. Do you think they look modern? I think they do, but we haven’t a clue of what they are saying. Maybe
there are messages, but we don’t know what these messages are. These pebbles are known as Azilian pebbles. [Present chart 2 – Crossing of Lake Superior]

And they we think people started using pictures for leaving messages or very important events. This message is all done in pictures. It is was still painted on a rock, and it is meant to remember something that happened. It was about an expedition that went across a large lake. It tells us this expedition had a certain amount of boats, and we can even count how many men were in each canoe. (About 16 in each boat). The first canoe was guided by a chief, whose totem
r symbol is a king fisher. A rather beautiful bird.

The expedition lasted three days, can you find three days on the chart? Yes, here we have three heavens and three suns. Three suns is like three days. We also see a land turtle. This turtle tells us that the people came back to land. And this has been painted so that everyone can remember this very important
ccasion. But would you be able to understand this message if no one
explained it to you. [Present chart 3 – The men that left to hunt]

I want to show you another message using pictures. This is a message that has been left for people who aren’t there. Look at the first man there. How many fingers does he have? This is saying three of us is going away to hunt animals. We’re going away for three days, how do we know that, goodbye, goodbye – and then we come back, hello!
This way of recalling events and leaving messages is being done through pictures. We do think of it as picture writing. Picture writing was done all over the world. [Present chart 4 – Pictograms]

People tried to communicate through pictures. What is interesting that even in many different parts of the world, the pictures were quite similar. These pictures are from North America, Egypt, and Asia. These are all signs. What do you think these could be? The sun, the sky, the rain, fish, water, and human beings. The pictures are very similar even if they come from many different parts of the world. Why could that be? Well because what they were observing in nature looked rather similar no matter what part of the world, they were in. But as time went on, people weren’t fully satisfied with this way of communicating. How much information can you give with these pictures? And think of all the time it takes. People wanted to express more in less time. So their pictures started to represent not just objects, but also ideas. And if that is the main purpose, then do we always have to draw so carefully and beautifully? Over time, what people wanted to draw became wider and wider, and the drawings became simpler, and they became stylized. So simple and stylized that people couldn’t understand what was being drawn. This also depends on what people were using to make the drawings. Here we have an example [Present chart 5 – Sumerian signs/ideograms]

These are examples of very stylized and simplified drawings. We can start to think of them as sings, rather than pictures, we think they came from the Sumerians. The Sumerians lived a long time ago, but not as long ago as the Stone Age. The Sumerians are an ancient civilization. And they lived in the part of Asia that is the closest to Europe. Some people call it the Middle East, on a plane between two rivers. Sometimes we call that land Mesopotamia, which means land between two rivers. These rivers are the Tigris and Euphrates. There is a lot of clay found between those two rivers. So the Sumerians used tablets made of clay to record their symbols. The instruments used to press into those clay tablets, we can call them a stylus. Writing using a stylus, helped them to draw or write in a simpler way. (Note: Their drawing and writing started to look very wedged shaped, Sumerian writing is known as Cuneiform writing, from the Latin word “cumeus” for wedge shaped) After they used their stylus to make the drawing and signs in the clay, then they baked the tablets and the clay tablets became very hard, hard like stone. They lasted so well and so long that we can find their tablets to this day. So many tablets have been found from this area of the world that we can speak of libraries of clay tablets.

Let’s look at this, this was originally a circle, representing the sun. Now look at the three marks inside, each line is a mark for ten. This represented a whole month. Now look at this one, what does it remind you of? That looks like a boot. This meant to rest, or to stay or remain. Like you are remaining in one spot. The next sign is the sign for an opening. It almost looks like a zipper. Now we are going to go to a completely different part of the world. Let’s go to Mexico. [Present chart 6 – Itzcoatl]

This is a long time ago in Mexico, when there was also an ancient civilization, called the Aztec Civilization. There was a very famous person called Itzcoatl. What is interesting about this name, if we take it apart, Itz means knife and Coatl means serpent. So, if I take Itzcoatl name apart, it means knife serpent. Can you see this picture? It is a serpent and a knife. Because back then they had

stone knives. That is a very easy way of remembering his name, this is picture writing. Even if I don’t know the Aztec language, can we guess what this means? And now something else can be done with his name, what happens if we take it apart into three parts. Itz – stone knife, Co – pot, Atl – means water. So, if these are the picture you give me, if might mean “knife pot water”. But I don’t think an important king would like that. But if I know that Aztec language, I know that together they give me Itzcoatl, they very important person, but to know that I must know the spoken language. [Draw eye, wave, bird, fly] This is where we combine pictures with spoken language. Now I am going to draw. First, I draw an eye. Do you ever like to go to the sea? Draw something that makes you think of the sea. (waves of the sea). And now let’s take a picture of a bird. And now let’s take a picture of a fly. We have the eye, the sea, a bird, and a fly. (I see a bird fly). To interpret this, we need to know our spoken language. [Draw pen, man, ship] Let’s draw another one. Draw a picture of a pen, a man, and a ship. (Penmanship) What is really important about this, is that they look like pictures, but to know the meaning you must know the spoken language. This was an incredible step forward, because we have a connection to the spoken language. Connecting words to pictures long ago was very new, and a very important step. Around the time of the Sumerians, there was also a very important civilization, the Egyptians. Let’s think for a moment about the Egyptians. They lived along a very long river, named the Nile River. They had many signs as well, they carved them in stone, in woods, and had a special material called papyrus. They would also paint on papyrus using brushes and ink. Their signs looked like pictures, and they were made very carefully. These are the signs they would carve, and there were called hieroglyphs [Present chart 7 – Egyptian hieroglyphs]

This means sacred carvings. What we are seeing on this chart is a set of signs that help the people understand the hieroglyphs. Because otherwise it is like a secret code, we can understand some things, but not everything. Sometimes they mean sounds, and sometimes they are just pictures. This actually means Cleopatra. This is the name of a very famous Egyptian Queen. All of these have

a sound associated with them. The Egyptians were using these signs for sounds, but the sings at the end tell us that she was a woman. The fact that the whole thing is in this frame tell us that she is very important. Only rulers could have their name in a frame like this, it is called a Cartush.

The Egyptians used these signs in all sorts of ways, for sounds, parts of words. How many sounds can you hear in “Pema”? We could use it for syllables and whole words as well, this was a very mixed system and these signs served a mixture of purposes. Idea writing, picture writing, and sound writing.

Now let’s think of another group of people, this other group lived around the same time as the Egyptians and there were called the Phoenicians. If you go all the way around the eastern end of Mediterranean, that’s where the Phoenicians lived. These people were great sailors and traders (Phoenicians were based in Lebanon). They were merchants, buying and selling things in different places. They were in fact truly excellent sailors and navigators. Some people say they sailed around Africa. Even if they stayed in the Mediterranean Sea, they could go between Asia, Africa and Europe and were constantly carrying things with them from one place to another. They traded many precious things, ivory, silk, papyrus, and in their own land they had some important cities. One of their very important cities was called Tyre.

Something they traded from their land was a dye called Tyrian purple. This was a very precious dye and very much sought after by royal people. Many people thought that the Phoenicians were very important because of all the sailing, trading, and their Tyrian Dye. But they were more important for a different reason, these Phoenicians came into contact with many different people. They knew about the Egyptian writing, how it was a mixed system, they liked it and wanted, but they were very busy people, and they really needed to keep precise and accurate records. Lists of what they were selling and buying, they needed a clear simple way to record, and because of that they came up with a very important idea. The idea that the signs would only be used for sounds. This writing could look like picture writing, but it was actually sound writing. All their signs represented sounds. Their signs looked like pictures, but they were not representing pictures or ideas, only sounds.

The Phoenicians had 22 signs that they used for sounds. We could have hundreds and thousands of pictures for signs, but these Phoenicians made it very simple. They could have taken it from the Egyptians, or from other people, but it doesn’t really matter. The way the Phoenicians used them, they just stood for sounds. Because the Phoenicians were very interested in saving time, thesigns became very stylized, they looked less and less like pictures and more and more like signs.

[Draw an Ox head and simplified sign] Let’s look at a Phoenician drawing that is actually a sign. Take a picture of a drawing of the head of an ox, and then look at it in a much simpler way without all the detail. It could be orientated differently. The Phoenicians word for ox was aleph and their word for house was beth. And when they looked at these signs, they pronounced the sound associated with the word. The Phoenicians traded with the Greeks, and the Greeks thought these signs for writing were great. And they took on the Phoenicians signs and that the idea that the signs should be associated with sounds. But they had a different language, and they didn’t call the same sounds the same. The called it Alpha-Beta. When we actually say alphabet, we are saying Ox house. But did we get the idea from the Greek? No, they got it from the Phoenicians. What is amazing, is that they all used the signs that came from the Phoenicians. [Turn A upside down] Many of the sings are similar. All the Phoenicians signs were for sounds like (p, and c) - all their signs were for consonants. Their language was rather special and they could get away with that, but the Greeks needed sings for sounds (A, e, i, o u ) for vowels. So, the Greeks changed it a bit. And that’s why we can say the Greek completed the alphabet, because they added the music to it. And when it was passed on to the Romans, the sounds were all there. But the Romans made the sings more beautiful, and rounded all the signs [Hang alphabet chart] We can see that very beginning of the alphabet originated with the Phoenician’s alphabet. [Place a and b from the movable alphabet on the mat]

We know the story of this letter “A” was for ox, and the letter “B” was a sign for a house. And this is story of our alphabet. You know that with these signs, (show the movable alphabet) we can send message all around the world. We can hear someone speak to us from long ago. And that is with the help of this story
f the ox and the house.

There are many versions of this story as are the charts being used. The story given in Bergamo, is the original story as indicated by Mario Montessori and the charts recommended by him.
“Formation of man” – Chapter 3 is a very good reference for language.
As this is a cosmic fable, it is presented early in the year.

The aim is also to show the simple but powerful way of the alphabet. The passage from picture writing to sound writing helped to make the written language so simple. The number of sounds in a language is always limited.
The story comes early for the children, as when we say long ago we don’t give a reference in time (Phoenician alphabet is around 3000 old and the Greek one is 5000 years old)
“This conquest is much greater and more important than any other for the progress of civilization. It was this achievement that could unify humanity across all of the succeeding generations.”
The written language constitutes the perfect way to help the human being benefit from all the discoveries made in the past.
The charts are not in a chronological order, are just showing the stages in the evolution of the written language.

The ancient Egyptians had 3 scripts: hieroglyphic (sacred carving), hieratic (priestly) and demotic (of the people). As the Egyptians passed to papyrus they used hieratic which was more “cursive”. The texts also had the hieroglyphs.
To arouse the children’s interest in the letters and where they came from. The story has been developed to appeal to the interest of an elementary child
To re-inspire the children who still need to work with the basics of the written language.
To help the children understand that we inherited the alphabet from the generations that came before us. It is a treasure that has been passed by generation to generation.

children.title: Word Study

blocks.text: The children can information about the words in the dictionary: spelling, etymology, parts of speech and pronunciation. When we think of words we think of the function
f words/parts of speech. Word study deals with word formation. Linguists do not talk

about sounds, they use the term phonemes as they are stricter about what a sound is. The linguists talk about graphemes instead of letters and the words are morphemes. An affix is an attachment to the word and the affixes have meanings. For example “– ly” that can be attached to “man” transforming it in “manly”. If an affix it is placed at the end of the word it is called a suffix and if it is placed at the beginning it is called a prefix. The affixes have to be attached to a word and cannot exist as a standalone, however they have a meaning. Some languages have also infixes, English language does not have.
In the English language the children can also explore a wide range of compound words (e.g. dragonfly)
Maria Montessori said that with whit work the children acquires a fortune, not in land
r gold but in language.

When two words are used together to yield a new meaning, a compound is formed. Compound words can be written in three ways: as open compounds (spelled as two words, e.g., ice cream), closed compounds (joined to form a single word, e.g., doorknob), or hyphenated compounds (two words joined by a hyphen, e.g., long-term). Sometimes, more than two words can form a compound (e.g., mother-in-law). The most common spelling question/debate writers face is whether to write compounds as separate words, one word, or hyphenated words.
