children.title: Children’s Language Work
Introduction

blocks.text: Written language

The major difference between the written language and the spoken language is that with the spoken language the other person participating in the conversation can ask for what’s not clear, meanwhile with the written language the requirement for correct use is higher. The children to understand this aspect and if possible to get accustomed to first write a draft and after continue with the final work. The written language is a very important tool of self-expression, this is why it is important to take great care about its development. The first experience children have with the written language is in Children’s House with the movable alphabet, later with the small movable alphabet and in the end with writing with the pen on paper.

In the Elementary classroom the children are offered factual writing, stories and poetry. Their work with the written language it doesn’t stop here: letters, petitions, short stories and even their own comic art work. All these require a good command of the spelling and punctuation. The children should’ve acquired most of these skills from their years in the Children’s House, but when the children arrive to the Elementary classroom their skills have to be assessed by the guide, through observation, to ensure that he picks up with the work from where the child really needs. The guide can help the children to improve their spelling, always having in mind, that they should be corrected in a gentle way as soon as the error is found. The children can write the corrected words in their own spelling dictionary. In Elementary they will also do word study which will help them to become aware of the homophones and other particularities of the spelling and pronunciation.
The children should be offered different kinds of literature to read, so they can draw inspiration, develop their language skills and technique.

To help the children develop their written language skills, the guide can help the children to understand that they can use adverbs or adjectives to describe, use rephrasing and punctuation marks to convey their ideas, stories in a more clear, fluent and readable fashion.
While writing their own compositions, the children should be encouraged to check the dictionary for any doubts they might have about the spelling or the meaning of a word.

The guide should read aloud in the classroom different kind of genres of literature, fictional or factual. The books should offer a good example of language. He can share with the children an excerpt of a book that he liked. The reading sessions should induce the respect and love for literature and the art of writing.

The factual writing of the children can have as a topic the biography of a famous author/scientist/ sportsman, can be a description of an animal or even factual writing about the lessons that they’ve got in the classroom in the last week/month.

Reports can be written and they can contain information from the outdoor activities, visits of a natural park or a museum. The reports can pave a way for the future research work, which can be done by the older children. The research work should be given the proper importance, respect and the children should understand that research is not just a way to copy facts but more a quest to find answers to an initial question.

The children between 6 and 12 years old are attracted to write prose, poetry and drama plays. The classroom should have a rich library and good supplies for writing and creating the artwork to necessary to decorate the work of the child.

It is interesting for the children to have an actor from time to time to guide and offer ideas and hints for their own plays or a play that they’ve read and want to perform for their peers in the classroom or for a large audience.

The children can have a lesson on writing letters and how the content of the letter changes depending on who’s the letter addressed. The children can participate in pen pal exchanges to make new friends, learn about the other’s culture and practice their language skills.
Another work that the children can do is to create timelines with different themes of their interest.
Punctuation is being introduced with the previous work of language, E.g. function of words, conjunction. Then later it can be introduced/revised in a context.
The aim of the work in the Elementary is to instill a love and appreciation for the written and oral language.

For practicing the handwriting the children can use small black boards with different linings, or paper that has in a light colour in the central area. To make the children aware of the slanting of the letters, the guide can use a fine red pencil to mark the line for the slanting.
Spoken language

For the spoken language the children should be encouraged to engage in coversation from a young age, making sure that the adult is really listening to them – not only pretending. The vocabulary that the adult uses should be rich and he as an adult should not fear that some of the words are unknown/hard for the child – children love to learn new words and being talked as they are really taken seriously.

The children should learn the power of the communication, how the words have to be measured and thought about before being released in a conversation or remark. The same words in different contextes can have total different meanings, can be healing or extremly hurtful for the conversation partner.

The children between 6-12 years old love to communicate, and this natural tendency should not be stopped but instead the children should learn how to communicate in a respectful matter with the others that share the same space with them. The communication in the classroom should be in low voice and during the Montessori work time should be related to their work or daily activities/duties.

The children use the spoken language to communicate while working together and therefore there is a constant exercise for their communication skills, which can bring benefits if the material that they are using offers opportunities for good/point on conversation (E.g. a good book for research, or a material with rich language).

Respect comes before the right of expressing one’s oppinion. The children should understand that with the spoken language, there is an easy and fast way to communicate, but communication doesn’t mean only speaking but also listening. During a conversation one has to respect the right of communication of the other part, respect their oppinion/view even though you don’t agree with.
Debate can be a great tool for the older children (9-12 years old) as debate opens the gates for research, critical thinking and improving their speech skills in front of their peers or an audience.

Reading aloud can be a challanging activity which will lead to the improval of the speech skills of the children. Reading aloud helps the children to improve their diction, reading speed and it is an indirect preparation for drama.
The work in the classroom should be always done in acordance with the sensitivities
f child corresponding to his developmental subplane/plane. “We should not speak so that it is possible for the audience to understand us, but so that it is impossible for them to misunderstand us.”
Marcus Fabius Quintilian

Gender of the nouns
In the English language there is only logical gender (depends on the sex). The grammatical gender is the one given to the objects in some language (E.g. “la mesa” in Spanish)
The logical gender in English can be masculine, feminine, neutral and common gender. (E.g. stallion, mare, horse, stable)

There is a gender scale that one can be aware of. We always say “Mary’s hat”, “The leg of the table”. The higher a noun is on the gender scale more common it is the use “’s” for the possession. Classification of the singular and plural in English language
How the plural is formed in English language
Plural formed by adding “s” – E.g. car - cars
Plural formed by adding “es” and pronounce it as “s” – E.g. church- churches
Plural formed by adding “s” and pronounce it as “es” – E.g. case – cases
Nouns ending in “o” – adding “s” or “es” – E.g. potato – potatoes and piano-pianos
Nouns ending in “f” or “fe” – adding “s” or “es” – E.g. chief – chiefs; scarf- scarves
Nouns ending in “y” – adding “s” or “es” – E.g. boy – boys; scarf-scarves
Nouns ending in “en” – adding “en” – E.g. child – children
Internal changes E.g. tooth- teeth
No changes E.g. sheep, deer
Compound words E.g. mother in law – mothers in low

Exotic plurals E.g. formula – formulae, vertebra – vertebrae, nebula – nebulae, focus – foci, aquarium - aquaria, media – medium, datum – data, vertex – vertices, matrix – matrices, tempo – tempi, graffito – graffiti.

blocks.text: “All about names. Proper, common, collective, material, abstract nouns. I want to tell you something about the noun. I want to interest the children in the study of nouns. We can easily think of the study of names. Language relates to human experiences and human psychology, as soon as human beings become interested in something, they want to communicate this interest to others. In order to do so, they need words, they need names. So, to whatever interests them they give names. Whenever human beings feel an emotion, these feelings also receive names.

Whenever a child is born, this child receives a name. In olden times, the names that were chosen had to do with the psychology of the people living at that time. If there were certain people who had helped the tribe, when the people of the tribe were in a difficult situation, whenever there were people who did great deeds, the names of these people might be given to the newborn child. In early times, there was so much need for protection, and so little understanding, that it was very understandable that they would use the names of these people who helped the tribe. People thought the name of the person was the soul of that person. Mario Montessori says when one is not paying attention, when they hear their name, they immediately pay attention.

It is as though the soul of this one person could be transferred to the newborn as a source of protection. As time went by and people understood more, naming became less about protection and more about affection. It also came to be more of an admiration to the new born.

People used the names of people they admired. Other people in India and other places, give names from nature. You may find that someone was moved by the beauty of a flower or its scent. You may find Violet being given as a name. Other were touched by other aspects of nature and you will find other names. Then again, it’s not so much the original calls, it’s kind of a connection to someone who was a part of the family who have since passed away.

On this chart you can see a grandfather and a grandmother, and all the people. Here is a list of the names that this newborn could have been potentially given. People have names of fruit, names of plants, names of virtues, with every new wave of people brings new sets of names. Then there are other names still. There are many names coming from old Greek (Phoebe), names from flowers Lilly, Rose, names from stone, some even come from the calendar. Then there are all the Christian names. Then there are names coming from the animals – Leo, Leonora, Robin. Others come from the stars. Those that come from the Hebrew. These names become a sort of living monument to someone who lived earlier.”

“The name is something that distinguishes one person from another. There are so many people that have the same name in the town, there is another distinction that can be made. I remember, someone came to me and said “John has broken his arm. I said, “Who? John the carpenter?” And he said, “No, John the tailor.” That was before family names. Because of these old distinctions that were made, you will find people such as Mr. Sheppard, Mr. Brewer, Mr. Carpenter, Mr. Painter, and Mr. Farmer. You will find
people named Mr. Head, Mr. Leg, Mr. Strong. All these names served to distinguish
ne person from another. There are other names which came from the names of some
things that they were either represented or there virtues. Mr. Hog could have been
riginally used for someone who looked after pigs or was as greedy as a pig. There is

another type of name which is especially common here, which was a way from distinguishing one person from another by saying who the father is. John the son of Robert – John Robertson. Macdonald – son of Donald, -Fitzgerald – son of Gerald. Imagine a Mr. Smith, he is the lord of London. And a beggar named Mr. King. This is a very impressive way of showing the children the name remains no matter what state the person becomes. Another factor is Mr. Churchill – church on a hill, Mr. Roosevelt which means pink field.”
Mario Montessori

Exploration for the classification of the nouns (Age group: 6-9 years old) Names Ancient world

In the ancient world, particularly in the ancient near-east (Israel, Mesopotamia, Egypt, Persia) names were thought to be extremely powerful and act, in some ways, as a separate manifestation of a person or deity. This viewpoint is responsible both for the reluctance to use the proper name of God in Hebrew writing or speech, as well as the common understanding in ancient magic that magical rituals had to be carried out "in [someone's] name". By invoking a god or spirit by name,
ne was thought to be able to summon that spirit's power for some kind
f miracle or magic (see Luke 9:49, in which the disciples claim to have

seen a man driving out demons using the name of Jesus). This understanding passed into later religious tradition, for example the stipulation in Catholic exorcism that the demon cannot be expelled until the exorcist has forced it to give up its name, at which point the name may be used in a stern command which will drive the demon away.
Quranic names (Arabic names)

We can see many Arabic names in the Quran and in Muslim people. Like the names Allah, Muhammad, Khwaja, Ismail, Mehboob, Suhelahmed, Shoheb Ameena, Aaisha, Sameena, Rumana, Swaleha, etc. The name Mohammed and Ahmed are same, for example Suhel Ahmad or Mohammad Suhel are same. In Islam and in Christianity we can see many similar names like (the first name is Islamic name and the second name is Christian name Islamic/Christian) Adam/Adam, Yusuf/Joseph, Dawood/David, Rumana/Romana, Maryam/ Mary, Nuh/Noah, etc.
Biblical names

In the Old Testament, the names of individuals are meaningful, and a change of name indicates a change of status. For example, the patriarch Abram and his wife Sarai were renamed "Abraham" and "Sarah" at the institution of the Abrahamic covenant (Genesis 17:4, 17:15). Simon was renamed Peter when he was given the Keys to Heaven. This is recounted in the Gospel of Matthew chapter 16, which according to Roman Catholic teaching was when Jesus promised to Saint Peter the power to take binding actions. Throughout the Bible, characters are given names at birth that reflect something of significance or describe the course of their lives. For example: Solomon meant peace, and the king with that name was the first whose reign

was without war. Likewise, Joseph named his firstborn son Manasseh (Hebrew: "causing to forget")(Genesis 41:51); when Joseph also said, "“God has made me forget all my troubles and everyone in my father's family.” Biblical Jewish people did not have surnames which were passed from generation to generation. However, they were typically known as the child of their father. For example: ‫ ישי בן דוד‬(David ben Yishay) meaning, David, son of Jesse (1 Samuel 17:12,58).
Talmudic attitudes
The Babylonian Talmud maintains that names exert a mystical influence
ver their bearers, and a change of name is one of four actions that can
avert an evil heavenly decree, that would lead to punishment after
ne's death. Rabbinical commentators differ as to whether the name's

influence is metaphysical, connecting a person to their soul, or bio- socio-psychological, where the connection affects his personality, appearance and social capacities. The Talmud also states that all those who descend to Gehenna will rise in the time of Messiah. However, there are three exceptions, one of which is he who calls another by a derisive nickname.
Surname

The name is something that distinguishes one from another, as the names might repeat, the people start to use the family names (surname) to distinguish one person from another who have the same first name. Surnames have not always existed and today are not universal in all cultures. This tradition has arisen separately in different cultures around the world. In Europe, the concept of surnames became popular in the Roman Empire and expanded throughout the Mediterranean and Western Europe as a result. During the Middle Ages this practice died
ut as Germanic, Persian, and other influences took hold. During the late

Middle Ages surnames gradually re-emerged, first in the form of bynames (typically indicating individual's occupation or area of residence), which gradually evolved into modern surnames. In China surnames have been the norm since at least the 2nd century BC. A family name is typically a part of a person's personal name which, according to law or custom, is passed or given to children from one or both of their parents' family names. The use of family names is common in most cultures around the world, with each culture having its own rules as to how these names are formed, passed and used. However, the style
f having both a family name (surname) and a given name (forename)
is far from universal. In many cultures, it is common for people to have
ne name or mononym, with some cultures not using family names. In

most Slavic countries, as well as other countries including Greece and Iceland, for example, there are different family name forms for male and female members of the family. Issues of family name arise especially on the passing of a name to a new-born child, on the adoption of a
common family name on marriage, on renouncing of a family name and on changing of a family name.
Classification of the nouns (Age group: 9 -12 years old)
The nouns classify in:
Concrete nouns
Common
Proper
Material (water, wood, etc.)
Collective
Abstract nouns
Quality
State
Action

The function of the words (parts of speech) depends on the context and it can be listed in a dictionary under different parts of speech E.g.: “round” can be a noun, adjective, preposition. Without a context it is impossible to classify a word. This deeper investigation is called parsing.
The aim of the work is to explore the language and not to transform the children in grammarians. The goal is to help the children think, reason and discuss.
Maria Montessori had a third classification for the nouns: spiritual noun for the nouns like God, angel, soul etc. (symbol: a black triangle with a golden circle)
Most of the material nouns are considered non-countable nouns.
General
To help reading become total reading - reading with full understanding and appreciation of the language. Grammar as a help to reading. Reading is an indirect help to writing.
To reinforce the understanding of the different functions the words.
To help the children to begin to explore each part of speech more deeply. This is a preparation for classifying a part of speech. A preparation for the parts of speech.
Noun/article grammar box
It can be with certain filling boxes a work of spelling (E.g. plural of the noun)
To help the children to become more aware of the language and think. The goal is to get the children think and not to find a definite correct answer.

children.title: Presentation of the “Introduction with the story”
Introduction of the kinds of adjectives with the story
Tell the story of the race in the park

blocks.text: I want to tell you a story of a race run by children in a park. This is a certain kind
f story and I will talk, and you will imagine and have all these pictures in your

mind. Let’s imagine we are in a park, what can we see, what do we hear, what do we feel, and what can we sense? A beautiful, warm day. A blue sky. A bright sun. A light breeze. Short, rough grass. Young children in the park laughing and talking. Teachers young and old, male and female, busy with their tasks. And there are trees. Slender, leafy trees, swaying ever so slightly in the breeze. Thick, solid, thin, slender, gnarled. Old trees, motionless, except for their dancing leaves. Silent, except for their rustling leaves. Plants and bushes with brilliantly coloured flowers. There is a lake there too. What else do we see? The rippling movement of the water in the lake. There are birds flying around in the park. We hear the sounds
f the birds in the park. Sweet, high pure notes and low chords. Different kinds
f birds singing different kinds of songs and doing different kinds of things.

Caged birds and birds which are free. Birds flying in the air. Swimming on the lake, running along the ground, resting, perching. Ornamental birds with splendid plumage. A loud whistle, a sudden silence, and hushed voices. The race has started. Which child will win? All are waiting to see. Which child will it be? The first child crosses the tape to take first place. The second child to cross the finish line will take second place. The third child to cross the finish line will take the third place. The winner of the race is the first child. This child is the winner. The winner is this child.

Time for lunch! A teacher distributes lunch boxes among a group of children. One for you, one for you, one for you. He gives a lunch box to each child; each child has a lunch box. After lunch, there is prize giving. The winner goes up to the special table to receive the prize. There is loud applause as the teacher hands the child the silver cup and says, “This is your cup because you ran so well”. The child takes his cup. He can hardly believe it, he thinks this is my cup, it is so beautiful.

The children point at the birds and recall the adjectives used

The guide says that we used a lot of adjective to describe everything, these are descriptive adjectives.
The guide talk about the race, the guide says that “which” is an adjective that we use when we ask a question: we can think of it as an interrogative adjective
The guide talks about the end of the race and the order at the end “first”, “second”, “third” – he says that these are adjectives too and have to do with the order so we call them ordinal adjectives.
The guide talks about the number of the children in the race and introduces the concept of numeral adjectives
The guide talks about the fact that we talked in the story about pointing out the winner – the adjectives that have this function like “this”, “that” we can think of it as a demonstrative adjectives
The guide talks about the lunch in the story and that the teacher distributed the boxes, we can think of adjectives like “each”, “every” as a distributive adjectives

The guide says that at the end there was a cup but it wasn’t someone’s cup – during the ceremony that cup became the winner’s cup – it was his cup. So we can think of adjectives like “his” “her” as possessive adjectives.

children.title: Comparison of the adjective

blocks.text: When we introduce the children to this work we want to guide them to think about the function and formation of the comparatives. The formation of the comparison is done with suffixes (inflexional method) added to the adjective, by adding words like “more”, “most” and with irregular formations like “good, better, best”. The words like “more”, “most” are adverbs and accompany the adjective. In the Children’s House the children are given the language for the comparison of the adjective after they worked with the sensorial material.

Prepositions:
Simple: for, by, at, out, in, of, off, through, till, up, to, with
Compound: amongst, amidst, above, around, along, across, about, below, beneath, beside, between, beyond, outside, within, without
Phrase: in front of, in the middle of
Prepositions according to functionality:

Prepositions of time: These prepositions denote time in the sentence. For example, look at the table below to get an idea of how prepositions of time are used. (E.g. “I went backpacking in Europe in 1999.”)
Prepositions of place: These prepositions denote a place in the sentence. (E.g. “Martha is in the car”)
Prepositions of direction: These prepositions show the direction of something. (E.g. “All students walked towards the assembly hall.”)
Prepositions of agent: These prepositions act as an agent between a noun and usually a verb. (E.g. “Hannah graduated with an honours degree”)
Prepositions of instruments, machines or devices: These prepositions connect instruments, machines or devices in the sentence. (E.g. “My brother opened the lock with a hairpin”)

There are two types of conjunctions: coordinate and subordinate conjunctions. Coordinate conjunctions always join clauses of equal rank and subordinate conjunction join clauses of different ranks. (E.g. “I love you and you love me.” /”She left five minutes because she was not feeling well.”)
Coordinate conjunction can be classified in:
Cumulative/additive/copulative: joining E.g. “and”
Adversative: contrasts E.g. “but”
Alternative: choices E.g. “or”
Illative: inference E.g. “for”
Subordinate conjunction can be classified in:
Time: E.g. “while, when, as soon as”
Condition: E.g. “if, providing, unless”
Reason: E.g. “because, since”
Purpose: E.g. “so, so that, so as”
Concession: E.g. “although, even if”
The conjunction neither nor comes always in a pair.

blocks.text: The overview of the language work:

children.title: Working with the B2 box – From the question to the names
Series 1 – Verb and Subject

blocks.text: The subject of a sentence or clause is the part of the sentence or clause about which something is being said. It is usually the doer of the action. It is a noun or a pronoun.
The verb or simple predicate is the word or words that expresses action or says something about the condition of the subject.

Predicate it is the part of sentence that tells us something about the subject. Everything that it is not the subject it is the predicate in English. Predicate comes from the Latin Pre+dicere for “in front to tell of” – to make something publically known about the subject.
Sentence analysis material
B2 – All parts (From the questions to the names)
Questions on one side and the name on the other side
No duplicates in the box
Question form
Form for B2: Question, Answer, Name of the part of the sentence
Folder with collection of sentences. Collection of prepared sentences for the reading analysis from child’s national literature. The collection is divided in series with simple sentences:
Series 1(A/B/C): Simple sentences
A: E.g. “The boy sang”
B: E.g. “He greeted and smiled”
C: E.g. “The lady and gentleman walked”
Series 2(A/B/C/D/E): Sentences with direct object(s)
A: E.g. “The boy lowered his head”
B: E.g. “Mary and John folded the mat”
C: E.g. “We dusted the door and the windows”
D: E.g. “Jacob and Martha picked the clothes and blankets.”
E: E.g. “Miss Miller touched my cheek and she smiled.”
Series 3: Sentences with indirect object(s). (E.g. “She sent Jim a card”)
Series 4: Sentences with adverbials. (E.g. “She sat trembling on a chair”)

blocks.text: A direct object is a noun or pronoun that receives the action of a verb or shows the result of the action. It answers the question "What?" or "Whom?" after an action verb. An action verb with a direct object is called a transitive verb.
The action of the verb falls directly on the direct object, this is why the arrow is on the same line with the arrow for the subject.

The indirect object it is involved in the action of the verb in a less direct way, in an indirect way. This is why it is found at an angle.

children.title: Story of spoken language

blocks.text: This story of the spoken language it is given to the children at the end of the first cycle, the beginning of the second cycle. The story of the Ox and the House it is important for the children who are not fluent readers, as it helps to reignite the interest in the written language. Historically the spoken language came before the written language, however the written language it is more concrete. The alphabet it is a concretization of the sounds of the language. The children have to have plenty of time to explore their language before exploring this story, they have to become acquainted with etymologies and sentence analysis.

In the first part we would like to make the children think of the spoken language in general before leading the children into the particular aspects of their language. The articulate language it is specific to the human beings and it can be considered as a fourth gift given to the human beings. Homo sapiens have always had language, however not everyone agrees on how much the other species in our genus homo had used the spoken language.

A human baby when born has the potential to learn any language, however he will limit the acquisition of sounds to the ones required for his language. The spoken language brought great advantages to the human beings in their history. It allowed the human groups to communicate, as they had to survive as social creatures. Coming back to the babies, we can certainly say that no baby can develop fully if his is isolated from his group.

The first introduction of the spoken language in general it is speculative, however it does not matter as the aim is to make the child think about the power of the spoken language. The second part it is meant to help the child localize the language in the whole and the third part it is the language of the child.

children.title: The origins of the spoken language

blocks.text: No materials

children.title: Presentation of the “The origins of the spoken language”
Talk about the different theories of the origins of spoken language

blocks.text: The guide says that today we are going to think of a great gift that we have. The great gift of speaking. It isn’t it true that we speak all the time. Can you imagine one day without speaking – you can try that. Have you ever thought how the spoken language came to be? Where, when and why? For all the things that came into being we had a story, what about the spoken language. No one knows exactly when the human beings started to speak but everyone believes that the human beings of the past, did speak. Speaking is and always was a characteristic of the human beings like us. Coming back to the idea of not speaking for one day – try it – do not answer when someone talks to you or when you want something, ask it without speaking. Maybe at the end of this day we would really appreciate what an incredible gift, speaking is. It is amazing that only the human beings have this ability, the animals communicate but they cannot really talk to us when we go back home. Maybe the cat will meow but definitely it is different than how we speak.

children.title: Introduction of the “Bow-wow” theory

blocks.text: Do you remember where the people where for the first time? Africa. We think that language started there but no one knows for sure. There are many theories about how language came into existence and some have funny names. There is one that says that language started like imitation, like the sounds of the animals – that we copied them like the sound of a dog, cat or bird – we call this sounds onomatopoeic – we got this word from the Greeks. Can you imagine how we could communicate as hunters like this? This idea it is called “The Bow-wow theory”. This theory can explain how some of our words evolved, but we cannot say that for all the words.

children.title: “Fl” theory

blocks.text: Some other linguists have realized that for some words there is a theme, for example: the words that are connected with the fire have the sound “fl” like flame, flare, flash or flicker. Can you think of any “fl” words that do not have anything to do with fire, so again this is an idea but we do not have to agree.

children.title: “Pooh pooh” theory

blocks.text: There is also another theory related to the interjections as when we let our emotions be expressed by our mouths like “Aaaa”, “auch”, “oooh” – it is a good theory to explore the interjections however we can explain the rest of the words just a few of them. This was called the “Poo poo theory”.

children.title: “The sounds of the effort” theory

blocks.text: Let us imagine a group of people working with a lot of physical exertion, a work that has to be coordinated and when we do hard work we sometimes we do noises, we hold our breath and later we let it go and a sound it is produced. These sounds form a pattern, consonsonant – vowel – consonant – vowel. This can take us to think of patterns in language. In English many syllables have the pattern consonant – vowel – consonant, so perhaps this theory has something
f truth when thinking of the evolution of the spoken language. If this happens

when working maybe the people had to communicate when working hard. Some of these sounds may have been developed into commands, a very easy way to communicate when working. If we agree with this theory we can think
f language as being developed in cooperation with the other human beings.

children.title: “Gesture” theory

blocks.text: Another idea that the people had is that language it tied to the gestures. Do you know any gestures? – the child shows. So as you can see that language developed from the gestures, some had developed a maybe more than others. It seems that parts of the brain that produce the gestures are linked with the
nes that produce speech – so maybe the gestures could have been a

beginning. Using gestures would be great for silent communication, as when the people would go hunting. Great for hunting – but how do you communicate like this in pitch dark at night or when the other person is around the corner. Some people say that hand gestures are accompanied by lip gestures.

children.title: “Music came first” theory

blocks.text: Some people think that before language there was song, the people would sing instead of talking. This idea was started by a Danish man talking about the English language. He felt that the “Bow-Wow” and “Pooh Pooh” theories explained parts of the language. He sustained that in the language we use intonation and pitch. He thought that further back we go, more pitch we get when studying language – so from this his idea came that the people sang before spoke. Singing is a way to express your emotions so there are language that use a lot the pitch: the Chinese (5 tonnes), the Cantonese (7 tonnes), the Vietnamese (9 tonnes).

children.title: “Contact” theory

blocks.text: A long time ago the people thought that the language developed due to the contact instead of communication. According to this theory the people did sounds like a wolf in the night. Only with time that became an expression of someone’s need to communicate with other people.
It is not important if these theories are correct, they should just invite the children to think of different aspects of language.

children.title: Presentation of the “The origins of the spoken language”
Introduction of the origins of the languages, dialects vs. languages

blocks.text: The guide says that today we want to think of our spoken language: English. Do you know where our language comes from? Have you heard other languages beings spoken? Have you been to other countries? If we hear other people speak a different language it is quite impressive, it sounds like a secret language. When we listen to other languages, what does it strike you the most? For me it is how different they sound, just because we do not understand. People who dedicated their life to studying language, they say all languages are related and they form different families. Many of the European languages and some of the Asian languages are grouped in one family. To do so they found certain words in all these languages that are similar. These words are basic words, very useful in the daily life: words for the family, for the body parts
r numbers. They looked at these words and decided that they must all come

from a single parent language. How is it that possible for a language to give birth to many other languages? Well, we have to imagine a big human group that speaks a language and they separate and move to different places. At the beginning they speak the same language, however with the time their lives are going to be different, they are going to experiment different situations so their language will change and adapt to the place where they live. Languages change all the time, even the language that we know speak with the time changes. If there is contact in between them then they will share their new words, however if they are going to be isolated from each other. If the differences are not great we call that
versions of the language: dialects. If the differences are great then we have two different language.

children.title: Inspect the charts 1, 2, 3, 4 and discussion

blocks.text: The guide says that the linguists spend time looking for words that are similar in between languages. Let us look at the chart with Latin, Greek, Sanskrit and Gothic and Old English.

The guide says that the linguists are interested to reconstruct that first original language might’ve sound. For English it is part of the Indo-European family of languages. Indo can make you think of India, and you are right as on this chart we have Sanskrit an old language.
The guide says that the Indo-European family is part of the Proto Indo European family.

The guide says that if we have an Indo-European language then we should’ve had a group of people who spoke this language. The scientists think that they might have lived in the Central European plains. After some time they might have moved away.
The guide brings the chart with the explosion and dispersion and says that it might have been like this.

The guide continues saying that the scientists think that they raised cattle, horses, dogs, might have used carts, had tools and weapons made of stone and from the common words we know they were familiar with wolves, bears but not elephants or tigers. They had words for river, streams but no words for
ceans or seas. For these people the family was important, from the words they

They liked to live in the forests, they liked to live apart from each other, they grew crops and their families were very important. They loved to fight and if a chief lost in battle he could not return home. All of these we know from the poet Tacitus. As they loved their space they spread all over Europe: Eastern Germanic: Gothic which with the time disappeared. The North Germanic and from there the languages: Swedish, Norwegian and West Germanic: English among others.

children.title: Presentation of the “Story of the English language”
Story of the English language
Tell the story of English

blocks.text: The guide says that we know that English is a Germanic language which closest neighbour is Friesian which is spoke on the coast of Netherlands. The story of English it is wrapped up with the story of England. When it comes to England or Britain there have been many people that lived in Britain. We are going to be thinking now about the British Isles. The people living on the main island, Britain, were called Britons. They were called Celt people around 2000 years ago. English language does not have anything to do with the Celtic language: this is why there is a story here. The people living there spoke Celtic. What it is that it happened that they changed their language?

children.title: Romans invade the Celtic – beginnings of the Old English

blocks.text: There lived happy Celtic people but at some point they got invaded by the Romans, and became part of the Roman Empire. The Romans brought their civilization with them, they built roads, built villas and even built a great wall: the Hadrian wall. The Romans brought many comforts. They also brought their language with them: Latin.

The romans stayed in Britain for almost 400 years, so the Celts started to speak a Latin version of Celtic. The got used to the romans defending their land – the Celts kind of forgot to defend themselves. As the centuries past, by the 5th century, things were not going great in Rome so the roman legions left and returned to Rome.

children.title: Angles, Saxons and Jutes invade Britain

blocks.text: The now Roman Celtic people got invaded by the Angles, the Saxons and Jutes who brought with them the Germanic languages. The Celtic languages end up around the fridges of Britain, Northern part, Ireland and Wales.

These new people coming into England did not speak Celtic and the Angles, Saxons and the Jutes set up in the part which we today call England. The language that they spoke in between them was what we call today the Old English.

The Germanic people brought with them a new languages, they all spoke different dialects and set up different kingdoms in England. So England ended up with 4 dialects, 3 of which are: West Saxon, Northumbrian and Mercian.

These dialects were competing with each other. Each one developed its own literature. In the end having a literature is very important in terms of how important a language is. It’s the West Saxon who managed to preserve their literature.

Angles settled in North England, speaking a Northumbrian dialect which gave us the very word for England. Therefore the name of our language. (The name “England” is derived from the Old English name Englaland, which means “land
f the Angles”.)

children.title: The arrival of the Vikings

blocks.text: At some point the Vikings came by sea to England and they destroyed the literature in their raids burning down the temples where it was safeguarded. They didn’t only raid and went away. They settled in the North of England so the English language still has Viking words like skirt or shirt. The Angles in the North they came under the influence of the Vikings. The Angles brought a lot
f words to the English language, but the Mercians are the ones that influenced
the most the Old English language. You see, English is fruit of many cultures coming together and each living its part, some of them still alive today.

children.title: Norman invasion in 1066

blocks.text: Let us get back to our story. Later in the 11th century is an important date for the English language: the year 1066. This year is going to bring English in a new period. By the year 1066 all the dialects merged into a single language: Old English. The Old English language was a phonetic language and it had many terminations.

Oh, yes I was saying something important happened. Well in 1066 the Normans invaded England from Normandy in France. They spoke an earlier version of French and this became the high status language in England. It brought many new words into English such as cash, age and reward, for instance. The Norman French became the language of the ruling class. French comes from Latin and it was nothing like the language the common people spoke in England. French and Latin became the language for education, the church, the government and so on. So popular was the Latin language that even the scientists published their books in Latin, Newton with his book “Prinkipia” being one of them.
Yet here is a point that English could have become French. English could have died out. We can think the story as the adventures of English, it almost went into extinct at various times.

children.title: Middle English

blocks.text: There came the time that Normandy was lost to King of France. The Norman French of England were considered as foreigners. The sons had to pledge loyalty to either the King of French or England.

There were no more invasions of England and gradually, almost 200 years later, English took over again from French. The English spoken around this time is called Middle English. A number of books were published in Middle English, perhaps the most famous one being a book of cracking stories called The Canterbury Tales by Geoffrey Chaucer. There are many words that come from the Norman French like foe, domicile, domestic, improbable, courageous. The Middle English language has become a language from two languages. The English language took a lot of words from the Latin not because of the Norman French but because the church was using the language.

children.title: Chart 1, 2 – Middle English and Modern English

blocks.text: The guide brings the chart with the chart 2 and reads with the child saying that the final “e” in the modern English it is there to remember us how to pronounce it.
Modern English: son (no ending)
Middle English: sone (not phonetic anymore, meaningless ending)
Old English: sunu (sun is phonetic, but with the Norman Scribe, the writing became son; meaningful ending)

The guide can look at other words with children: covering the ending and think whether it’s phonetic or non-phonetic; then think about the ending for the nouns and verbs: come – comen – cuman / love – loue - lufu

The guide says that the words that came from French and all the changes did not hurt the language, it just simplified it. What it became more difficult is the fact that the language is not phonetic anymore therefore the spelling can be sometimes more difficult to remember. This challenge helps us to remember the
rigin of the English language.
The guide and the child can inspect also the chart 1.

children.title: Modern English

blocks.text: The guide says that Modern English is here for over 500 years. Do you think that the English spoke 500 years ago it is same as now? No. Not only that English became Modern English but also we passed into a new age the Modern Age. A time of discoveries where Columbus explored the world, there is a rebirth of science, art, the scholars – we call it Renaissance. During the middle ages it is the church that dominated the people’s lives. People became interested in the Ancient Greek and Ancient Roman civilizations and ideas. People started to build in a classical style. Printing appeared in Europe and Gutenberg was the one that had the first printing press. William Caxton was the first to bring printing to England. Printing has had an enormous influence on language. This invention changed how the books were made. Before made by the scribes, monks who copied the books, most of the time in a place called Scriptoria in the monasteries. A book at that time, written by hand would cost as much as a house. They wrote with the quill feathers and ink. The most expensive material for writing was velum (from the calf skin). You see printing made the books accessible to so many people. It was like a revival for learning, there was so much going for art, literature, inventions. The printers had to choose the language to use in the books. They had to use a Standard English for printing that books. One spelling for one word and it was the printer who chose that spelling. When printed the words remained as they were decided by the printer. It is the written word that lasts. Here is another reason why the spelling is like it is, the way we pronounce a word changes but as soon as you write it stays in that way. The people still argue if the English language should be phonetic. For example in the Renaissance they wrote “debt” to show an homage to the Latin language “debitus” even though the word is pronounced “det” and this is only one example.

With the Renaissance also came the voyages of exploration and this meant a lot of contact with many people – peaceful or not. The English language, led to a lot of trade and colonization, who let the English in contact with many people. So the English language borrowed many words from other language (e.g. frankfurter, champagne, orange, caravan, paradise, chutney, Alleluia, zero, algebra, caliph, tea).

children.title: Shakespeare and conclusion

blocks.text: We know about the Old English, Middle English and about the Modern English. With all the voyages, the new words coming from faraway places or even from Latin or Greek we can talk about the beginnings of the Modern English. You might have heard about Romeo and Juliet, a play written by Shakespeare. If you are going to start reading Shakespeare that is the beginning of the Modern English. “Romeo, Romeo! wherefore art thou Romeo?”. Yes you are right it sounded a little bit different and that is because as we saw the language we speak is alive, it changes with each of us. However in its words you can discover hidden treasures, stories about long ago times and with every word we use become part of this beautiful history of the English language.
The English language has always kept an openness to another languages, an
penness that started a long time ago with the coming of the Roman people,
for this we just have to think that not even half of the words go back to the Old English.

children.title: Alternative story – [Not given in the course]

blocks.text: Where did the English we speak today come from? To find an answer we have to look at the history of the languages spoken in the British Isles because it takes a little while before it really becomes something we can call English.

children.title: 600 BC – The Celts

blocks.text: The first languages we know about in the British Isles are the Celtic ones like Welsh and Scots Gaelic. These people probably settled here about 600BC, that is more than 2500 years ago. English still has some borrowed Celtic words like corgi meaning 'little dog' from Welsh or whisky 'water of life' from Gaelic.

children.title: 55BC – The Romans

blocks.text: In 55BC there was an invasion by the Romans who spoke Latin. They gave Latin names to places and some of these names are still used today. For instance any place name containing 'chester' is derived from the Roman name for that place. It comes from their word for 'camp'. I bet you can think of a place name that has 'chester' in it.

children.title: 450AD – Anglo - Saxons

blocks.text: The first people who spoke the language which over time turned itself into English conquered England in about the Year 450. These people were known as Anglo-Saxon and their language is also often called Anglo-Saxon or Old English. Many words from this time are still around in English: cow, house, bread and sword.

children.title: 800AD – The Vikings

blocks.text: From about 800 the Vikings started to invade Britain. The Vikings came from countries like Denmark and Norway and spoke a language which later developed into Norwegian and Danish. The language the Vikings spoke left behind many words in English: you, husband, law and anger. Also places: Tenby and Grimsby in which the 'by' means village.

children.title: 1066AD – The Normans

blocks.text: In 1066 Normans invaded England from Normandy in France. They spoke an earlier version of French and this became the high status language in England. It brought many new words into English such as cash, age and reward, for instance.

children.title: 1400AD – Middle English

blocks.text: There were no more invasions of England and gradually English took over again from French. The English spoken around this time is called middle English. A number of books were published in middle English, perhaps the most famous
ne being a book of cracking stories called The Canterbury Tales by Geoffrey
Chaucer.

children.title: 1476AD – Printing Press

blocks.text: Books have been written in English since the 9th century, but it was with the introduction of the printing press by Thomas Caxton in 1476 that publishing really took off. With the printing also came an interest in a standard way of writing English which had not been present before.

children.title: 1525AD – The English Bible

blocks.text: In 1520 the New Testament of the Bible was translated into English by William Tyndale. This was quite a big step since it meant that people who only knew English could read the Bible themselves. The church didn't like this at all and so the first Bibles were printed elsewhere and smuggled into England.

children.title: 1550AD – Invading Words

blocks.text: England wasn't being attacked by armies anymore but words were still invading. In the 16th century there was great interest in studying as people read books written in Latin and Greek and they borrowed words from these languages. It is kind of strange since Latin was a dead language at this stage, no-one spoke it for day-to-day purposes.
Since this time, words have been coming into English in dribs and drabs. For example the Dutch were pretty nifty with boats and so words like cruise and yacht were also borrowed.

children.title: 1580AD - Shakespeare

blocks.text: There are many important authors in modern English, however one of the most well-known early writers is William Shakespeare (1564 - 1616). He deserves a mention here since many words in English are first found in his plays. It could be that he invented words or that he took words that were only used in spoken English and put them in print.

children.title: Today – Modern English

blocks.text: English has been shaped by many events and has been influenced by many different languages. One of the people playing a part in shaping English now is actually you! Every time you use a word or phrase that your parents would not have used you are helping to change English! For many languages, English is now the language to borrow from. French has “le weekend”, the word “business” is often used in Italian, Swedish cars now have an “airbag” and the Dutch word for goal is... You guessed it – “goal”!

English is divided in three periods:
Old English (5th – 11th century)
Beowulf
Beowulf (/ˈbeɪəwʊlf/; Old English: [ˈbeːo̯wulf]) is an Old English epic poem consisting of 3,182 alliterative lines. It is
ne of the most important works of Old English literature.

The date of composition is a matter of contention among scholars; the only certain dating pertains to the manuscript, which was produced between 975 and 1025. The author was an anonymous Anglo-Saxon poet, referred to by scholars as the "Beowulf poet"
Middle English (12th – 15th century)
Canterbury tales Geoffrey Chaucer

The Canterbury Tales (Middle English: Tales of Caunterbury) is a collection of 24 stories that runs to over 17,000 lines written in Middle English by Geoffrey Chaucer between 1387 and 1400. In 1386, Chaucer became Controller of Customs and Justice of Peace and, in 1389, Clerk of the King's work. It was during these years that Chaucer began working on his most famous text, The Canterbury Tales. The tales (mostly written in verse, although some are in prose) are presented as part of a story-telling contest by a group
f pilgrims as they travel together from London to
Canterbury to visit the shrine of Saint Thomas Becket at
Canterbury Cathedral. The prize for this contest is a free meal at the Tabard Inn at Southwark on their return.
Modern English (16th – 20th century)
Shakespeare

William Shakespeare (26 April 1564 – 23 April 1616) was an English poet, playwright and actor, widely regarded as the greatest writer in the English language and the world's greatest dramatist. He is often called England's national poet and the "Bard of Avon". His extant works, including collaborations, consist of approximately 39 plays, 154 sonnets, two long narrative poems, and a few other verses, some of uncertain authorship. His plays have been translated into every major living language and are performed more often than those of any other playwright.

In 1066 the Norman Conquest of England (in Britain, often called the Norman Conquest or the Conquest) was the 11th-century invasion and occupation of England by an army of Norman, Breton, Flemish, and French soldiers led by the Duke of Normandy, later styled William the Conqueror.
Old English was a highly inflected language: it had a lot of endings.
English continues to change and it is interesting to explore what happens with the British English and the other places where English is spoken.

blocks.text: The guide says that when this two sentences come together to a form a longer sentences each part can be called a clause.

children.title: Transposition and discussion

blocks.text: The guide does transpositions with the two sentences.

Note: In the case of the coordinated clauses the order is not important as usually the message can be understood even if the order is changed. However, sometimes the order can be important due to the logic sequence of the actions. children.title: Introduction of the concept: coordinate/collateral clauses

blocks.text: The guide after the children have worked for some time with the material can says to them that the clauses of equal importance are called coordinate clauses if they have at least one conjunction. If there is no conjunction we call them collateral clauses. (e.g. “See, buy, fly”)

children.title: Introduction of the concept: compound sentences

blocks.text: The guide says that the sentences formed by two coordinate clauses are called compound sentences.
Examples
Then he began to weep and tore his hair in anguish.
The transposition changes the meaning of the sentence.
He looked into the mirror, straightened his tie, smoothed his hair and went out to greet his two friends.

children.title: Complex sentences
Adjective clauses

blocks.text: A main clause is a clause that is not introduced by a subordinating term. It does not modify anything, and it can stand alone as a complete sentence. Main clauses are sometimes called principal or independent clauses.

A subordinate clause is usually introduced by a subordinating element such as a subordinating conjunction or relative pronoun. It depends on the rest of the sentence for its meaning. It does not express a complete thought, so it does not stand alone. It must always be attached to a main clause that completes the meaning.
Subordinate clauses normally act as single part of speech. They can be either noun clauses, adjective clauses, or adverb clauses.
They are sometimes called dependent clauses because they "depend" on a main clause to give them meaning.

An adjective clause is a subordinate clause that modifies a noun or pronoun. The italicized clause in the first sentence is an adjective clause because it modifies the noun clause. Most of the time adjective clauses begin with the relative pronouns that, which, who, whom, or whose.

blocks.text: This is the work that is found in the Children’s House section of this album. However, this work is suitable for the children in Elementary.
7 series of slips(differentiated by height) between 9 and 28 slips in each series:
Series 1: 16 slips with simple sentences (E.g. “The boy run away from his sister.”)
Series 2: 12 slips with two coordinated clauses. Two consecutive actions. (E.g. “He took of his hat and made a bow”) -
Series 3: 12 slips with sentences with two or more coordinated clauses (E.g. “He opened the door, peeked inside and started laughing loudly.”)
Series 4: 11 slips with complex sentences with one subordinated clause. (E.g. “When he made the drawing he kept examining the flower very carefully.”)

Series 5: 28 slips with sentences more involved, more complex, descriptive which may require pronunciation of words aloud. (E.g. “He dropped his back in his chair, his head sunk between his shoulders as he was very cold.”)

Series 6: 16 slips with more difficult interpretation with occasional speaking (E.g. “The woman, sat in her carriage, looking outside repeatedly like she was expecting someone to come and save her from a disaster.”)
Series 7: 6 slips with interpretation requiring more than one person. (“The boy run away from his sister.”)

children.title: Presentation of the “Interpretative reading”
Read silently, act with feeling – the other children guess

blocks.text: The guide invites the child to take a slip, read it silently and act with feeling as described in the text on the slip
The other children can guess what the “actor” is acting.
The guide can discuss with the children about why the actor had to do that action and what might have happened after the action was done.

children.title: Follow-up activities
Read the passage from the book

blocks.text: You can read from the book the passage illustrated in the slip to understand the context of the action and what happened before and after the paragraph from the slip.
There is an emotional charge in the text on the slip, the children have to act with emotion the scene presented.
The texts are excerpts from the classic literature of the child’s country.

The verbs in the text are in the indicative mood third person, so the child has to demonstrate something that is described. The child has to become an actor, read the script and interpret appropriately.
The child has to express the text in words, attitude and actions
To give the children the opportunity to read short excerpts from literature and to act
To encourage the love for reading
Preparation for drama
6-9 years old

children.title: Books and Library

blocks.text: The books in the environment have to been handpicked to ensure that the quality of the content is good. Each classroom should have a library with all the subject areas explored: geography, biology, history, art, music, language, mathematics, physics and chemistry. Having a library helps the children have a starting point in their exploration.
The books can be organized in a general library or can be organized on subjects around the classroom.
The classroom should have also a reading corner. A comfortable area for reading for pleasure and not necessarily for research.
Books should be well maintained and handled with care. The books represent the human knowledge and work therefore deserve a special respect and care.
The children can have presentations on how to make books and are encouraged to write their own booklets with the knowledge gained.

children.title: Notes on Style

blocks.text: “Proper words in proper places make the definition on style.” Jonathan Swift
“Style is the dress of words.“ Chesterfield
“Style depends on the perfect matching of the content.” Kenneth Rexroth
“Literature might be an art but writing is a craft and a craft has to be learned. Skill in matching intention and expression comes with practice” Kenneth Rexroth

This chapters serves to offer ideas on what to do with the children in order to help them understand style. Style is the way we put out thoughts together, the form in each we express our thoughts. Style is an individual aspect however it has general characteristics for good style. If someone considers a style to be good or not it is a personal decision.
This work has to be done with the children not only to help them appreciate literature, but because they are starting to develop their own style.
As the material we can use the grammar symbols, as the grammar symbols can reveal the style of a writing.

Most of the previous work has to do with analysis, looking at the function of each word in a particular context. A more detailed examination can be done with the sentence and clause analysis material. The symbols used have been choose to show the particular function of that word/part of sentence.

The indirect preparation is every important in the Montessori approach to education. The indirect preparation is feeding the unconscious mind at an earlier stage and with the later work it is just a process of taking the unconscious to the state of conscious.
The most important indirect preparation for style is the classical literature with a good style present in the work with interpretative reading, sentence reading and analysis.

Reading aloud is another important activity in the Elementary environment. The literature offered to the children has to be chose with care. The guide can choose different genre of literature: prose, poetry, drama and so on.
One of the great preparations for writing is reading.
There are factors that we can consider for a good style:
Grammatical structure
Grammar helps the children to become aware of the grammatical their
wn language. All the work that they do with word study, function,
transposition help the children appreciate other author’s style and create their own style.
Vocabulary
A good vocabulary it is important as the choice of words it is essential for a good style
Clarity in expression
A very important aspect if we want the others understand the text.
“We should not write for the reader to understand us but to so that it is impossible to misunderstand us”
The guide should propose many activities of understanding what they are reading. For example reading articles from the newspapers, different literature genre.
For clarity in expression the punctuation it is very important. The children should work with the punctuation during all the years for elementary.
Appropriateness
Content and form should be in harmony. A harmony between the “what” and the “how”.
For example when summarizing, the number of adjectives should be reduced to a minimum.
The writer has to have clear if the point of writing is descriptive or factual. The descriptive writing uses a lot of adjectives and adverbs to embellish the message sent.
Essence of style
The children can use sentence analysis to explore the balance of their own writing by separating the sentence into clauses. They can do the same thing by exploring the classical literature works.

In the first years the children develop their own style of writing and the help given is indirect and in the second part 9-12 the help offered is more direct. The guide and the child can discuss their writing style.
Symbols can reveal the pattern of writing. Exploring the literature in this way helps the children have a better understanding of the style used and the particularities of each genre.
There are no ready made presentations for this work. The guide can design its own presentations. Child’s own writing
We encourage the children to symbolize their own writing. For this they have to leave blocks of space for the adhesive grammar symbols.
Charts with poems/literature
The guide can prepare charts with factual and descriptive writings and the grammar symbols.
The charts can be displayed in the classroom and the presentation to be spontaneous.

Suggestions for Making Your Writing Understandable and Interesting From the Austin Community College

1. Write in coherent paragraphs. A coherent paragraph is a group of sentences all relating to one basic idea. The first sentence is often a topic sentence, meaning that it states the unifying theme that binds the sentences together. In a paragraph, each sentence should develop logically from the preceding
ne. Often, one should use "connector" words or phrases to make this logical
development clear to the reader.

2. Write paragraphs that are neither too short nor too long. Avoid paragraphs that contain only one sentence. If you have a paragraph that is more than about a half page in length, try to break it into at least two paragraphs.

3. Begin most sentences with the subject, rather than with a dependent clause, an adverb, or a prepositional phrase. Such devices may provide useful variety if used sparingly, but they often slow the natural flow of ideas.
Bad: John Smith, realizing that he had perhaps only one last
pportunity to bring order to a community torn by strife and lack of
bureaucratic efficiency, decided to assume absolute control over the Jamestown settlers.

Better: John Smith decided to assume absolute control over the Jamestown settlers, realizing that this might be his last opportunity to bring order to a community torn by strife and lack of bureaucratic efficiency.

4. Write with an economy of words. Communicate a fact, opinion, argument, etc. with as few words as possible. Good writers always follow this principle. Several of the following suggestions will contribute to developing a tight prose style.

5. Do not use empty, cliche words and phrases in your writing. These include "Generally," "in general," "basically," "it went as follows," "really," "it has been proven time and time again that . . .," "the fact of the matter is . . . ." Here is a very wordy example.
Bad: It is a safe assumption to state the idea that the attitudes of our forefathers have affected the entire course of history.
Better: Delete the first ten words. Begin the sentence with: The attitudes
f our forefathers . . . . . (Communicates the same idea much more
forcefully and directly.)
6. Avoid the passive voice wherever possible. Use the active voice instead.
Passive voice: President Lincoln was shot by John Wilkes Booth.
The same information, recast in the active voice: John Wilkes Booth shot President Lincoln.
(The passive voice is usually in the form shown in the first example: the word "was," followed by the past tense of the verb, followed by a preposition.)

Overuse of the passive voice is one of the most common style errors in college student papers. The passive voice is weak; things are happening to people rather than people doing things. Also, the passive voice is wordier, therefore more boring. (One cannot always avoid the passive voice, especially if the subject is not known, or if it would sound strange [or be wordy] to specify a subject.)

7. Keep sentences relatively short. Overly long sentences slow the reader down and can hide the writer's meaning. One way to keep sentences short is to avoid excessive use of dependent clauses. If a portion of your paper seems stiff and difficult to follow, count the number of dependent clauses. If several follow one after the other, rewrite.
8. Do not overuse adjectives. Properly used, adjectives can add interest and clarity. Too many adjectives, however, slow down the flow of your ideas.
9. Do not string together prepositional phrases in a sentence. It makes it difficult for a reader to understand what you are trying to say.

Bad: The civil rights movement of the post-World War II era among black activists in the South and sympathetic liberals in other parts of the nation and among some leaders in both major political parties was part of a progressive tradition aimed at elements of society with legitimate complaints against the prejudices of the majority of persons in twentieth-century America.

Better: The post-World War II civil rights movement attracted black activists in the South and sympathetic liberals throughout the nation and had the support of some leaders in both major political parties. It was part of a progressive tradition which sought to meet the legitimate complaints of persons suffering racial discrimination at the hands of many twentieth-century Americans.
10. Avoid using prepositional phrases conveying possession wherever possible. Change to the possessive form.
Wordy: The chief talent of Daniel Webster was his gift of oratory.
Better: Daniel Webster's chief talent was . . . .
11. Always use the past tense when writing about things that happened in the past.
Bad: The problem, as Houston views it, is how to keep his army intact. Meanwhile, Santa Anna pursues him relentlessly. (Change to viewed, was, and pursued.)
12. Avoid repeating words and/or phrases in close proximity to one another. Such prose is boring.
The following excerpt from an actual history term paper illustrates the problem:

It seemed the years of prosperity were to come to an end for Castroville. In the 1880s, Castroville rejected a proposition from a railroad company due to the cost and it was subsequently built five miles south of Castroville. This killed the freighting business of Castroville almost at once, and in 1892 the county seat was also moved to Hondo. Many of the people of Castroville moved to the new county seat, while others moved to San Antonio.
Better:

The situation changed in the 1880s, after Castroville rejected a proposition from a railroad company to construct a line through the town. It was subsequently built five miles south of the community. This quickly killed off the local freighting business. In 1892 the county seat transferred to Hondo. Many Castrovillians moved there, while others withdrew to San Antonio.

A particular case of the same problem: Avoid repeating pronouns referring to the same person throughout a paragraph (she, her, hers, she, she, her, etc.). This is boring. Solution: In some of the instances, use of the person's name, title,
r other words and phrases which identify the person.

13. Clarity demands that you identify important persons and terms in your paper. Your theoretical target reader is not your professor but a fellow college student who is not an expert on your subject or on history in general. Therefore, when you introduce a person in your prose, briefly identify him or her. Also, if you introduce a term that is not familiar to the typical college student, briefly explain it in the text.
Elegance in Writing Style
This is difficult to define and describe. Perhaps it is useful to suggest that elegant writing style is neither colloquial and "slangy" nor too much given to fancy,
polysyllabic words, either. It is graceful, aesthetically pleasing, and unobtrusive. Following are suggestions to help you write with in an elegant style.

1. Wherever possible, use short words (generally of Anglo-Saxon origin) rather than longer ones (often derived from Latin). In 1940 British Prime Minister Winston Churchill wrote to United States President Franklin Roosevelt, requesting war materiel to stave off defeat at the hands of Nazi Germany. These were his words: "Give us the tools, and we will finish the job." He did not say, "Deliver to us the implements, and we will complete the assignment." While the quotation is not taken from historical writing, it suggests that short words often move the reader along more effectively than long ones.
2. Do not use contractions in formal writing. Example: Alexander didn't end his conquests once he had liberated the Greek colonies of Ionia from Persian rule. (Write out both words, did not.)
3. Do not use slang or colloquialisms in formal writing.
Jackson was fixing to (change to about to) leave for his plantation in Tennessee but reconsidered when he heard what Calhoun had said.
Grant was drunk a lot of the time. (Change to much.)
4. In most instances, avoid using personal pronouns referring to you, the author
f the paper.
Examples:
It seems to me that Senator McCarthy should have realized that he had gone too far in his "witch-hunt" for suspected Communists. (Delete the first five words.)
Napoleon's greatest mistake, as I see it, was his invasion of Russia in 1812. (Delete the phrase set off by commas.)
